question: Which two capabilities does My Domain enable in the context of a SAML SSO configuration? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Login Forensics
optionB: App Launcher
optionC: Resource deep linking
optionD: SSO from Salesforce Mobile App
explanation:
Resource deep linking and SSO from the Salesforce mobile app are the two capabilities that depend on My Domain. My Domain gives the org a unique login URL, which is what lets a deep link to a specific record survive an SP-initiated SAML redirect — the target is carried in RelayState and the user lands on the intended resource rather than the home tab. The mobile app needs that same unique URL to know which org, and therefore which identity provider, to drive the flow against.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Login Forensics) — a monitoring and threat-detection add-on that reports on login activity. It neither requires My Domain nor plays any part in a SAML configuration.
Option B (App Launcher) — the tile list of apps a user can reach. It is not something a SAML SSO configuration enables through My Domain.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.domain_name_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000315559&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000386791&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers wants to implement SAML SSO for their internal Salesforce users using a third-party IdP. After some evaluation, UC decides not to set up My Domain for their Salesforce org. How does that decision impact their SSO implementation?
optionA: Neither SP- nor IdP-initiated SSO will work.
optionB: SP-initiated SSO will not work.
optionC: Either SP- or IdP-initiated SSO will work.
optionD: IdP-initiated SSO will not work.
explanation:
SP-initiated SSO will not work. Without My Domain, users arrive at the generic login.salesforce.com hostname, which is shared across every org, and Salesforce documents the consequence directly: when SSO starts from a Salesforce link — the login page, a deep link, an Outlook Sync URL — 'Salesforce does not know in advance which Identity Provider to use.' That is the SP-initiated case. IdP-initiated SSO is unaffected, because the identity provider posts the assertion straight to Salesforce's endpoint and the assertion itself identifies the audience.
One documented caveat is worth knowing rather than overstating the answer: on a generic login page, SP-initiated SSO can work after the user has completed at least one IdP-initiated SSO, because Salesforce then sets a browser cookie identifying the correct IdP for future logins. So the accurate claim is that SP-initiated SSO cannot be initiated on its own without My Domain — not that the flow is permanently impossible in every circumstance.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (neither SP- nor IdP-initiated SSO will work) — overstates it. IdP-initiated SSO needs no My Domain, since the IdP already knows which Salesforce endpoint to post the assertion to.
Option C (either will work) — understates it, and is the answer you reach by assuming the login hostname is irrelevant. It is precisely the shared hostname that leaves Salesforce unable to pick an IdP.
Option D (IdP-initiated SSO will not work) — has the two flows the wrong way round. IdP-initiated is the one that survives without My Domain.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000315559&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Key B stands. The explanation was right in substance but overstated: it said SP-initiated SSO 'cannot be triggered', full stop. The documentation adds a real caveat — for generic login page setups, SP-initiated SSO works once a prior IdP-initiated login has set a browser cookie identifying the IdP. Added that so the item teaches the actual mechanism (unique hostname enables immediate IdP lookup) rather than an absolute that the docs qualify.

question: How should an architect force users to authenticate with Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) for Salesforce only when not connected to an internal company network?
optionA: Use an Apex trigger on the UserLogin object to detect the user's IP address and prompt for 2FA if needed.
optionB: Apply the 'Two-Factor Authentication for User Interface Logins' permission and Login IP Ranges for all profiles.
optionC: Use Custom Login Flows with Apex to detect the user's IP address and prompt for 2FA if needed.
optionD: Add the list of company's network IP addresses to the Login Range list under 2FA Setup.
explanation:
A Custom Login Flow with Apex is what makes 2FA conditional on the network. A login flow runs after credentials are presented but before the session is established, and Apex inside it can read the user's source IP, compare it with the corporate ranges, and invoke the 2FA challenge only when the address falls outside them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Apex trigger on the UserLogin object) — Apex triggers are not available on UserLogin, and a trigger could not interpose a challenge partway through authentication in any case.
Option B (the 'Two-Factor Authentication for User Interface Logins' permission with Login IP Ranges) — that permission forces 2FA on every UI login unconditionally. Login IP Ranges beside it restricts where a user may log in from at all, rather than varying the challenge by location.
Option D (adding the company IP addresses to a Login Range list under 2FA Setup) — there is no such list in 2FA setup. IP ranges live on profiles and in Network Access, and neither makes the second factor conditional.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_login_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_networkaccess.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A multinational industrial products manufacturer is planning to implement Salesforce CRM. They have the following requirements: (1) Implement Partner Communities for their partner network; (2) operate in multiple countries with multiple Salesforce orgs; (3) some partners do business in multiple countries and need information from multiple Salesforce communities; (4) provide a single login for partners. How should an Identity Architect solution this requirement with limited custom development?
optionA: Register partners in one org and access information from other orgs using APIs.
optionB: Create a partner login for the country of their operation and use SAML federation to provide access to other orgs.
optionC: Consolidate partner-related information in a single org and provide access through a Salesforce community.
optionD: Allow partners to choose the Salesforce org they need information from and use login flows to authenticate access.
explanation:
A partner login in the country of operation, federated to the other orgs with SAML, meets all four requirements with limited custom development. It keeps the existing multi-org footprint, gives each partner one home org where they are provisioned, and uses SAML federation so that authenticating once at that org grants SSO into the other country communities — a single login across the network delivered by configuration rather than code.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (register partners in one org and reach the others by API) — API callouts move data between orgs but do nothing about authentication, so partners would still face separate logins, and building and maintaining those integrations is the custom development being avoided.
Option C (consolidate partner information into a single org) — solves the problem by re-architecting the multi-org landscape the requirements take as given. A consolidation programme of that size is far more than limited development.
Option D (let partners choose an org and use login flows to authenticate) — a login flow runs after Salesforce has already authenticated the user in that org, so it cannot supply the cross-org single login, and driving the choice per session is custom work.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identity_provider_enable.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has an existing web application that it would like to access from Salesforce without requiring users to re-authenticate. The web application is owned by UC and the team responsible for it is willing to add new JavaScript code and/or libraries to the application. What implementation should an architect recommend to UC?
optionA: Create a Canvas app and use Signed Requests to authenticate the users.
optionB: Configure the web application as an item in the Salesforce App Launcher.
optionC: Add the web application as a Connected App using the OAuth User-Agent flow.
optionD: Rewrite the web application as a set of Visualforce pages and Apex code.
explanation:
A Canvas app authenticated with Signed Requests is the recommendation. Canvas is purpose-built for embedding an external web application inside Salesforce without a second login: Salesforce posts a signed request carrying the user's identity and session context to the canvas iframe, and the canvas SDK on UC's side validates the signature and establishes the session from it. It depends on being able to add JavaScript to the external application, which UC's team has agreed to.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an item in the App Launcher) — a tile is only a link. The user still arrives at the web application unauthenticated and is asked to log in, which is the requirement being avoided.
Option C (a Connected App using the OAuth User-Agent flow) — still runs the user through an OAuth authorization redirect rather than passing the existing Salesforce session across, and the token it returns is for calling Salesforce APIs rather than for signing the user in to UC's own application.
Option D (rewrite the application as Visualforce pages and Apex) — reaches the outcome by discarding the application the scenario keeps, and is the most expensive option on the list.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_connect.meta/platform_connect/canvas_framework_intro.htm

question: A farming enterprise offers smart farming technology to its farmer customers, including sensors for livestock tracking, pest monitoring, and climate monitoring. They plan to store all the data in Salesforce and ensure timely maintenance of installed sensors. They have engaged a Salesforce architect to propose an appropriate way to generate sensor information in Salesforce. Which OAuth flow should the architect recommend?
optionA: OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow
optionB: OAuth 2.0 Asset Token Flow
optionC: OAuth 2.0 Device Authentication Flow
optionD: OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer Token Flow
explanation:
The OAuth 2.0 Asset Token Flow is the flow built for this. It issues short-lived, JWT-based asset tokens to connected devices and registers each device as an Asset record in Salesforce, so readings arrive attached to the asset that produced them — which is what makes maintenance of the installed sensors trackable rather than merely storing the data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SAML Bearer Assertion Flow) — exchanges an existing SAML assertion for an access token on behalf of a user a SAML IdP has already authenticated. Livestock and climate sensors have no SAML identity.
Option C (Device Authentication Flow) — is for input-constrained devices that a person is pairing, such as a TV: it displays a user code the person enters elsewhere. It authorizes on behalf of a human and creates no Asset record.
Option D (JWT Bearer Token Flow) — a server-to-server flow in which a pre-authorized client asserts a signed JWT for a known user. It could push data in, but it issues no per-device token and links no device to an asset.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_asset_token_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) built a Customer Community for customers to buy products, review orders, and manage their accounts. UC has provided three different options for customers to log in to the Customer Community: Salesforce, Google, and Facebook. Which two role combinations are represented by the systems in the scenario? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Facebook is the Service Provider and Salesforce is the Identity Provider.
optionB: Google is the Service Provider and Facebook is the Identity Provider.
optionC: Salesforce is the Service Provider and Facebook is the Identity Provider.
optionD: Salesforce is the Service Provider and Google is the Identity Provider.
explanation:
Salesforce is the Service Provider, and Facebook or Google is the Identity Provider. The customer is trying to reach the Customer Community, so Salesforce is the resource being protected and is therefore the Service Provider throughout. Choosing to log in with Facebook or with Google hands authentication to that service, which asserts the resulting identity back to Salesforce — making each of them an Identity Provider in this scenario.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Facebook is the Service Provider and Salesforce the Identity Provider) — reverses the roles. Nobody here is logging in to Facebook using a Salesforce identity.
Option B (Google is the Service Provider and Facebook the Identity Provider) — describes a login between two of the identity providers that never happens. The three login options are alternatives to one another, not a chain.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_authentication_providers.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is implementing a new Experience Cloud site and the identity architect wants to use dynamic branding features as part of the login process. Which two options should the identity architect recommend to support dynamic branding for the site? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: To use dynamic branding, the community must be built with the Customer Account Portal template.
optionB: An external content management system (CMS) must be used for dynamic branding on Experience Cloud sites.
optionC: An Experience ID (expid) or placeholder parameter must be used in the URL to represent the brand.
optionD: To use dynamic branding, the community must be built with the Visualforce + Salesforce Tabs template.
explanation:
Dynamic branding turns on one documented mechanism: the Experience ID. You extend the identity endpoints with an expid value — site-url/services/oauth2/authorize/expid_value and site-url/idp/endpoint/HttpPost/expid_value — or pass expid={value} on the login page, CommunitiesSelfReg, and forgot-password URLs, and Salesforce resolves the brand-specific logo and content from that value at run time. That is option C.
The other half is that the site must be one you can brand in Experience Builder. Every Experience Cloud template except Salesforce Tabs + Visualforce is a Lightning template customised in Experience Builder, and each one 'comes with its own set of pages for login, identity verification, password resets, and self-registration'. That is option A.
Be aware that option A is narrower than the documentation: nothing restricts dynamic branding to the Customer Account Portal template specifically. Read A as 'a Lightning/Experience Builder template, of which Customer Account Portal is one' — that is the claim the docs support.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an external CMS must be used) — states a requirement that does not exist. A CMS URL is merely one place an expid placeholder can point; the branding itself is resolved by Salesforce from the Experience ID.
Option D (the Visualforce + Salesforce Tabs template) — is the one template that rules dynamic branding out, because it is not built or branded in Experience Builder and has none of the Experience Builder login pages to brand.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.external_identity_dynamic_extend_endpoint_expid.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=experience.external_identity_create_branded_experience.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A,C stands as the best-supported pair, but the item is partly defective and the explanation now says so. Option C is solidly documented. Option A is not: 'Brand Your Experience Builder Pages' never mentions the Customer Account Portal template at all, and states that *each* Experience Cloud template ships its own login/verification/reset/self-registration pages. The real requirement is an Experience Builder (Lightning) template — which is why option D, Salesforce Tabs + Visualforce, is the genuine exclusion. A is defensible only on the loose reading 'a Lightning template such as Customer Account Portal'; flagged rather than silently confirmed.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters manages application functional permissions centrally as Active Directory groups. The CRM_SuperUser and CRM_Reporting_SuperUser groups should respectively give the user the SuperUser and Reporting_SuperUser permission sets in Salesforce. Salesforce is the service provider to a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) identity provider. How should an identity architect ensure the Active Directory groups are reflected correctly when a user accesses Salesforce?
optionA: Use a login flow to query standard SAML attributes and set permission sets.
optionB: Use a login flow to query custom SAML attributes and set permission sets.
optionC: Use the Apex Just-in-Time handler to query standard SAML attributes and set permission sets.
optionD: Use the Apex Just-in-Time handler to query custom SAML attributes and set permission sets.
explanation:
The Apex Just-in-Time handler reading custom SAML attributes is the mechanism. Active Directory group membership is not one of the standard SAML claims, so the IdP has to send CRM_SuperUser and CRM_Reporting_SuperUser as custom attributes in the assertion. The SAML JIT registration handler runs during user creation and update from that assertion, which is where those attributes can be read and the matching permission sets assigned on every login.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a login flow querying standard SAML attributes) — wrong on both halves: group membership is not a standard attribute, and a login flow runs after authentication rather than as part of provisioning the user from the assertion.
Option B (a login flow querying custom SAML attributes) — has the right attributes but the wrong hook. The login flow is not the component that provisions and updates the user from the assertion.
Option C (the JIT handler querying standard SAML attributes) — has the right hook but the wrong attributes. There is no standard claim carrying AD group membership for it to read.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A leading fitness tracker company is getting ready to launch a customer community. The company wants its customers to login to the community and connect their fitness device to their profile. Customers should be able to obtain exercise details and fitness recommendations in the community. Which should be used to satisfy this requirement?
optionA: OAuth Device Flow
optionB: Named Credentials
optionC: Single Sign-On Settings
optionD: Login Flows
explanation:
The OAuth Device Flow is what connects the tracker to the customer's profile. It exists for devices with limited or no input capability — a fitness band cannot host a login form — so the device displays a short user code and the customer completes the authorization in the community on a phone or browser, after which the device holds a token bound to that customer's account.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Named Credentials) — a Salesforce-side store of an endpoint and its authentication settings for outbound callouts. It secures calls Salesforce makes to other systems, not a device authorizing itself into the community.
Option C (Single Sign-On Settings) — configures federated login for users arriving from an identity provider. It does nothing for a device with no browser to redirect.
Option D (Login Flows) — runs extra screens or logic after a user authenticates. It can shape the login experience but cannot pair a device that never presents credentials.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_device_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.remoteaccess_oauth_device_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses a legacy Employee portal for their employees to collaborate and post their ideas. UC decides to use Salesforce Ideas for voting and better tracking purposes. To avoid provisioning users in Salesforce, UC decides to push ideas posted on the Employee portal to Salesforce through API. UC decides to use an API user using OAuth Username-Password flow for the connection. How can the connection to Salesforce be restricted only to the Employee portal server?
optionA: Add the Employee portal's IP address to the Login IP Range on the user profile.
optionB: Use a dedicated profile for the user the Employee portal uses.
optionC: Add the Employee portal's IP address to the IP Relaxation / Trusted IP Range for the Connected App.
optionD: Use a digital certificate signed by the Employee portal server.
explanation:
The integration authenticates with the OAuth Username-Password flow, and the only documented mechanism that denies a login by source IP is a profile's Login IP Ranges: 'To control login access at the user level, specify the ranges of allowed IP addresses on a user's profile. When you define IP address restrictions for a profile, a login from any other IP address is denied.' Putting the Employee portal server's address in the API user's profile Login IP Ranges is therefore what restricts the connection to that one host.
The Connected App setting named in option C does not do this. A connected app's trusted-IP field is labelled 'Trusted IP Range for OAuth Web Server Flow' and governs the web server flow, not the username-password flow used here. IP Relaxation is a relaxation control — its options bypass the org's IP restrictions rather than impose them — and Salesforce notes that IP restrictions are enforced only when they are configured on a user's profile, which points back to option A.
A note on the scenario itself: Salesforce is retiring the OAuth 2.0 username-password flow for connected apps, and says the update 'will break all connected app integrations that use this flow'. The IP-restriction answer above is unchanged, but a design like this one should now move to the client credentials flow for server-to-server integration, or the web server flow with PKCE for end-user login.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a dedicated profile for the portal's user) — sound practice, and the profile is where the ranges are configured, but a dedicated profile on its own restricts nothing.
Option C (the Connected App's IP Relaxation / Trusted IP Range) — governs the web server flow and relaxes restrictions rather than imposing them, as set out above.
Option D (a digital certificate signed by the Employee portal server) — certificates play no part in the username-password flow; that is how a client authenticates in the JWT bearer flow.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_profiles_epui_login_ip_ranges.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.connected_app_edit_ip_ranges.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005388592&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Answer moved C->A. The deck asserted that a Connected App's "IP Relaxation / Trusted IP Range" restricts token requests to a trusted range. Rendering the documentation shows two things against that: the field is scoped to the OAuth Web Server flow by its own name ("Trusted IP Range for OAuth Web Server Flow") while this question specifies the Username-Password flow, and IP Relaxation exists to relax org IP enforcement, not to add it. Salesforce states IP restrictions are enforced only where configured on a user's profile, and the Restrict Login IP Addresses in Profiles article says outright that a login from any other IP address is denied. That is option A.

question: Which two security risks can be mitigated by enabling Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) in Salesforce? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Users creating simple-to-guess password reset questions.
optionB: Users accessing Salesforce from a public Wi-Fi access point.
optionC: Users choosing passwords that are the same as their Facebook password.
optionD: Users leaving laptops unattended and not logging out of Salesforce.
explanation:
Two-factor authentication defends the cases where the password alone has been exposed. A credential captured on a public Wi-Fi access point still cannot produce a login, because the attacker does not hold the second factor, and a password reused from Facebook is worth nothing to whoever obtains it in a breach of that site, for the same reason.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (simple-to-guess password reset questions) — a weak reset path is closed by password and reset policy, not by a second factor at login.
Option D (laptops left unattended and still logged in) — the session is already established and already authenticated, so nothing prompts for a second factor. Session timeouts and screen locks are what address this.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_require_two_factor_authentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_overview_2fa.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses a legacy Employee portal for their employees to collaborate. Employees access the portal from their company's internal website via SSO. It is set up to work with SiteMinder and Active Directory. The Employee portal has features to support posting ideas. UC decides to use Salesforce Ideas for voting and better tracking purposes. To avoid provisioning users on Salesforce, UC decides to integrate Employee portal ideas with Salesforce Ideas through the API. What is the role of Salesforce in the context of SSO, based on this scenario?
optionA: Identity Provider, because the API calls are authenticated by Salesforce.
optionB: Connected App, because Salesforce is connected with Employee portal via API.
optionC: Service Provider, because Salesforce is the application for managing ideas.
optionD: An independent system, because Salesforce is not part of the SSO setup.
explanation:
Salesforce is an independent system here, because it is not part of the SSO setup at all. The SSO described — SiteMinder against Active Directory — authenticates employees to the Employee portal, and Salesforce sits outside that flow entirely: employees are deliberately not provisioned in Salesforce, and the only traffic reaching it is the portal's server-to-server API call.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Identity Provider) — an identity provider authenticates users and asserts their identity to another system. Salesforce authenticates no one in this scenario; SiteMinder does.
Option B (Connected App) — a connected app is the record describing an external application to Salesforce, not a role Salesforce itself plays, and the question asks about the SSO topology rather than the integration.
Option C (Service Provider) — would be true only if employees were being signed in to Salesforce by the portal's IdP. No employee ever logs in to Salesforce here.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a mobile application for its employees that uses data from Salesforce as well as uses Salesforce for Authentication purposes. UC wants its mobile users to only enter their credentials the first time they run the app. The application has been live for a little over 6 months, and all of the users who were part of the initial launch are complaining that they have to re-authenticate. UC has also recently changed the URI Scheme associated with the mobile app. What should the architect at UC first investigate?
optionA: Verify that the Callback URL is correctly pointing to the new URI Scheme.
optionB: Validate that the users are checking the box to remember their passwords.
optionC: Confirm that the access token's Time-To-Live policy has been set appropriately.
optionD: Check the Refresh Token policy defined in the Salesforce Connected App.
explanation:
The Refresh Token policy defined in the Connected App is the first thing to check. Users are meant to enter credentials only once, which is what a refresh token delivers, and the cohort now being asked to re-authenticate is precisely the one that first authorized the app around six months ago — the signature of a refresh token set to expire after a fixed period rather than remaining valid until revoked.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the Callback URL and the new URI scheme) — a mismatched callback URL breaks the authorization redirect for everyone at once, not only for the launch cohort, and it fails the login outright rather than asking for credentials again.
Option B (users checking a box to remember their passwords) — no such setting governs this. Whether a password is stored in a browser or password manager has no bearing on how long the app's OAuth authorization lasts.
Option C (the access token's Time-To-Live) — an expiring access token is the normal case and is exactly what the refresh token silently replaces. If refreshing were working, a short access-token lifetime would never reach the user.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.connected_app_manage_oauth.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a mobile application that calls the Salesforce REST API. In order to prevent users from having to enter their credentials every time they use the app, UC has enabled the use of refresh tokens as part of the Salesforce Connected App, and updated their mobile app to take advantage of the refresh token. Even after enabling the refresh token, users are still complaining that they have to enter their credentials once a day. What is the most likely cause of the issue?
optionA: The refresh token expiration policy is set incorrectly in Salesforce.
optionB: The app is requesting too many access tokens in a 24-hour period.
optionC: The OAuth authorizations are being revoked by a nightly batch job.
optionD: The users forget to check the box to remember their credentials.
explanation:
The refresh token expiration policy is set incorrectly. A re-authentication landing once a day is the signature of a refresh token policy that expires after a fixed period or after a day of inactivity, rather than the 'Valid until revoked' setting a long-lived mobile app normally wants. The refresh token is working; it is simply being retired every 24 hours.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (too many access tokens requested in 24 hours) — hitting a limit on token requests returns an error from the token endpoint, and it would strike the heaviest users at unpredictable moments rather than everyone once a day.
Option C (a nightly batch job revoking OAuth authorizations) — fits the daily rhythm, but nothing in the scenario describes such a job. It invents a cause where a documented setting already explains the symptom.
Option D (users forgetting to check a box to remember credentials) — there is no such box in this flow. Whether the app must prompt is decided by the refresh token, not by a user choice at login.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_refresh_token_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.connected_app_manage_oauth.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has built a custom time tracking app for its employees. UC wants to leverage Salesforce Identity to control access to the custom app. At a minimum, which Salesforce license is required to support this requirement?
optionA: Identity Connect
optionB: External Identity
optionC: Identity Verification
optionD: Identity Only
explanation:
Identity Only is the minimum license. It gives an internal employee the Salesforce Identity services — single sign-on, the App Launcher, connected app access — needed to reach a custom application, without the CRM functionality a full Salesforce license carries. That is exactly what controlling employee access to UC's own time tracking app requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Identity Connect) — not a user license at all. It is the component that synchronises users from Active Directory into Salesforce.
Option B (External Identity) — the equivalent license for external users such as customers and partners. The users here are UC's own employees.
Option C (Identity Verification) — not a license granting access to an application. Identity verification credits are an add-on covering SMS and similar verification methods.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_licenses.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has an off-boarding process where a terminated employee is first disabled in the LDAP directory, then requests are sent to the various application support teams to finish user deactivations. A terminated employee recently was able to login to NTO's Salesforce instance 24 hours after termination, even though the user was disabled in the corporate LDAP directory. What should an identity architect recommend to prevent this from happening in the future?
optionA: Configure an authentication provider to delegate authentication to the LDAP directory.
optionB: Set up an identity provider (IdP) to authenticate users using LDAP, set up single sign-on to Salesforce, and disable Login Form authentication.
optionC: Create a Just-in-Time provisioning registration handler to ensure users are deactivated in Salesforce as they are disabled in LDAP.
optionD: Use a login flow to make a callout to the LDAP directory before authenticating the user to Salesforce.
explanation:
Standing up an identity provider that authenticates against LDAP, federating it to Salesforce with single sign-on, and disabling Login Form authentication is what closes the 24-hour window. Once LDAP disables the account the IdP will not issue an assertion, and with the login form switched off there is no Salesforce-local password left to fall back on. Closing that fallback is the part that actually removes the window, rather than merely narrowing it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an authentication provider delegating to LDAP) — names something that cannot be configured. Salesforce documents an Authentication Provider as a way to log in with credentials from a third party using OpenID Connect or a custom OAuth 2.0 configuration, and LDAP is neither. The feature that does validate credentials against an LDAP server is Delegated Authentication, configured under Single Sign-On Settings and backed by a SOAP web service you host; that would satisfy the requirement, but it is not what this option describes.
Option C (a Just-in-Time provisioning registration handler) — a JIT handler runs only when a user logs in, so a user who can no longer authenticate never triggers it and is never deactivated by it.
Option D (a login flow calling out to LDAP before authenticating) — a login flow runs after Salesforce has already validated the credentials, which is the wrong side of the check.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_authentication_providers.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer moved A->B. Option A says to "configure an authentication provider to delegate authentication to the LDAP directory", but Salesforce documents Authentication Providers as OpenID Connect or custom OAuth 2.0 integrations with a third party, with no LDAP support. The feature that validates credentials against LDAP is Delegated Authentication, which is a different feature and not what option A names. Option B is a complete, documented solution, and disabling Login Form authentication is what actually closes the bypass that left the 24-hour window. The deck's own structural audit flagged this as a near-miss: the explanation argued Delegated Authentication while the key pointed at the Auth Provider option.

question: Universal Containers (UC) currently uses Salesforce Sales Cloud and an external billing application. Both Salesforce and the billing application are accessed several times a day to manage customers. UC would like to configure single sign-on and leverage Salesforce as the identity provider. Additionally, UC would like the billing application to be accessible from Salesforce. A redirect is acceptable. Which two Salesforce tools should an identity architect recommend to satisfy the requirements? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: App Launcher
optionB: Connected Apps
optionC: Salesforce Canvas
optionD: Identity Connect
explanation:
A Connected App and the App Launcher are the two tools. The Connected App represents the external billing application to Salesforce and carries the SAML or OpenID Connect configuration that makes Salesforce the identity provider for it; the App Launcher then surfaces that connected app as a tile, so a user already signed in to Salesforce reaches billing by clicking it and arrives authenticated. A redirect being acceptable is what makes this pair sufficient.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Salesforce Canvas) — embeds an external application inside a Salesforce page rather than redirecting to it. It solves a harder problem than the requirement states, and needs code added to the billing application.
Option D (Identity Connect) — synchronises users from Active Directory into Salesforce. There is no Active Directory in this scenario, and it provides no path from Salesforce to the billing application.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_saml_sso.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An insurance company has a Connected App in its Salesforce environment that is used to integrate with a Google Workspace (formerly known as G Suite). An identity and access management (IAM) architect has been asked to implement automation to enable users, freeze/suspend users, disable users, and reactivate existing users in Google Workspace upon similar actions in Salesforce. Which solution is recommended to meet this requirement?
optionA: Configure User Provisioning for Connected Apps.
optionB: Update the SAML Just-in-Time (JIT) handler in Salesforce for user provisioning and de-provisioning.
optionC: Build a custom REST endpoint in Salesforce that Google Workspace can poll against.
optionD: Build an Apex trigger on the UserLogin object to make asynchronous callouts to Google APIs.
explanation:
User Provisioning for Connected Apps is the recommended solution. It is Salesforce's declarative provisioning feature: the connected app is linked to the target system, and Salesforce pushes enable, freeze, disable and reactivate events out to it as the matching action happens on the Salesforce user — the full lifecycle the requirement lists, without code.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a SAML Just-in-Time handler) — JIT runs only when a user logs in, and it provisions users into Salesforce from an incoming assertion. It is the wrong direction, and it cannot deprovision anyone, because a disabled user never logs in to trigger it.
Option C (a custom REST endpoint for Google Workspace to poll) — inverts the integration, makes Google responsible for noticing changes, and replaces a supported feature with code to build and maintain.
Option D (an Apex trigger on the UserLogin object making callouts) — triggers are not available on UserLogin, and a login-time hook would in any case miss every deactivation, which is precisely the event that produces no login.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_user_provisioning.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is creating a web application that will be secured by Salesforce Identity using the OAuth 2.0 Web Server Flow (this flow uses the OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant type). Which three OAuth concepts apply to this flow? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Client Secret
optionB: Scopes
optionC: Verification URL
optionD: Access Token
explanation:
Client Secret, Scopes and Access Token are the three concepts that apply. The web server flow runs on a server that can keep a secret, so the client secret is presented with the authorization code at the token endpoint to prove which application is asking; scopes are requested at authorization time and fix what the resulting token may do; and the access token is what comes back from that exchange and is sent on every call to a protected resource.
Why the other option is wrong:
Option C (Verification URL) — belongs to the OAuth 2.0 Device Authentication Flow, where a device with no browser displays a verification URL and a code for the user to enter elsewhere. The web server flow redirects the browser it already has, so it never issues one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_web_server_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.remoteaccess_oauth_device_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An identity architect works for a multinational, multi-brand organization. As they work with the organization to understand their Customer Identity and Access Management requirements, the identity architect learns that the brand experience is different for each of the customer's sub-brands, and each of these branded experiences must be carried through the login experience depending on which sub-brand the user is logging into. Which solution should the architect recommend to support scalability and reduce maintenance costs, if the organization has more than 150 sub-brands?
optionA: Create a community subdomain for each sub-brand and customize the look and feel of the login page for each community subdomain to match the brand.
optionB: Create a separate Salesforce org for each sub-brand so that each sub-brand has complete control over the user experience.
optionC: Use Audiences to customize the login experience for each sub-brand and pass an audience ID to the community during the OAuth and SAML flows.
optionD: Assign each sub-brand a unique Experience ID and use the Experience ID to dynamically brand the login experience.
explanation:
Assigning each sub-brand a unique Experience ID and branding the login experience from it is the scalable answer. One Experience Cloud site resolves the logo, images and content for whichever brand the expid value names, so 150 sub-brands become 150 configuration values against a single site to build, patch and maintain.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a community subdomain per sub-brand with its own customised login page) — works for a handful and collapses at 150: every branding change, security patch and template upgrade has to be repeated 150 times, which is the maintenance cost the question asks to reduce.
Option B (a separate Salesforce org per sub-brand) — the same problem an order of magnitude worse, adding 150 orgs to license, administer and keep in step.
Option C (Audiences, with an audience ID passed during the OAuth and SAML flows) — Audiences do vary what a page shows, by criteria such as profile or location, but they are an Experience Builder targeting feature rather than a value the identity endpoints accept. The parameter carried through those flows to brand a login page is the Experience ID.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_branding_use_cases.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.external_identity_dynamic_extend_endpoint_expid.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) would like to enable self-registration for their Salesforce Partner Community users. UC wants to capture some custom data elements from the partner user, and based on these data elements, wants to assign the appropriate profile and account values. Which two actions should the architect recommend to UC? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Modify the CommunitiesSelfRegController to assign the profile and account.
optionB: Configure registration for communities to use a custom Visualforce page.
optionC: Modify the SelfRegistration trigger to assign profile and account.
optionD: Configure registration for communities to use a custom Apex controller.
explanation:
The pair is a custom Visualforce registration page and a modified CommunitiesSelfRegController. The Visualforce page collects the custom data elements the standard registration form does not ask for, and the community's Login and Registration settings are pointed at it; the controller is where those submitted values are read and turned into the right profile and account assignment as the user is created.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (modify the SelfRegistration trigger) — there is no such trigger. Self-registration is handled by the registration page and its controller, not by a trigger Salesforce provides on registration.
Option D (configure registration to use a custom Apex controller) — the registration setting points at a page, and the controller comes along with the Visualforce page named in option B. As written this is the right idea one step out of place.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_self_registration_configure.htm&type=5&language=en_US
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_self_registration_modify_default_page.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is planning to build a new customer service portal and wants to use passwordless login, allowing customers to login with a one-time passcode sent to them via email or SMS. How should the quantity of required Identity Verification Credits be estimated?
optionA: Each community comes with 10,000 Identity Verification Credits per month and only customers with more than 10,000 logins a month should estimate additional SMS verifications needed.
optionB: Identity Verification Credits are consumed with each SMS (text message) sent and should be estimated based on the number of login verification challenges for SMS verification users.
optionC: Identity Verification Credits are consumed with each verification sent and should be estimated based on the number of logins that will incur a verification challenge.
optionD: Identity Verification Credits are a direct add-on license based on the number of existing member-based or login-based community licenses.
explanation:
Identity Verification Credits are consumed with each SMS sent, so the quantity should be estimated from the number of login verification challenges that will be answered by SMS. Delivering a one-time passcode by email consumes no credits, and that is what makes the SMS subset the right thing to count rather than logins or challenges in general.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (10,000 credits per community per month, with extra needed only above 10,000 logins) — invents an allowance and ties consumption to logins rather than to messages sent.
Option C (each verification sent, estimated from all logins that incur a challenge) — the closest distractor, and wrong in the direction that costs money: counting email verifications alongside SMS overstates the requirement and buys credits that will never be spent.
Option D (a direct add-on license sized by existing member-based or login-based community licenses) — credits are consumed by usage, not allocated per community license, so a per-license calculation bears no relationship to how many are needed.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_sms_identity_verification.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005239145&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers (UC) has decided to use Salesforce as an Identity Provider for multiple external applications. UC wants to use the Salesforce App Launcher to control the apps that are available to individual users. Which three steps are required to make this happen? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Set up Identity Connect to synchronize user data.
optionB: Add each Connected App to the App Launcher with a Start URL.
optionC: Set up an Auth Provider for each external application.
optionD: Create a Connected App for each external application.
optionE: Set up Salesforce as a SAML IdP with My Domain.
explanation:
The three steps are to set Salesforce up as a SAML identity provider with My Domain, create a Connected App for each external application, and give each connected app a Start URL so it appears in the App Launcher. My Domain is the prerequisite for acting as an IdP; the connected app is where each application's SSO configuration lives; and the Start URL is what turns that connected app into a launchable tile, whose visibility is then controlled per profile or permission set — which is how UC controls the apps available to individual users.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Identity Connect to synchronise user data) — synchronises users from Active Directory into Salesforce. No directory sync is described here, and it contributes nothing to publishing apps in the App Launcher.
Option C (an Auth Provider for each external application) — points the wrong way. An auth provider lets Salesforce accept identities asserted by an external service; here Salesforce is the one asserting identity outward.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_saml_sso.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identity_provider_enable.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is looking to purchase a third-party application as an Identity Provider. UC is looking to develop a business case for the purchase in general and has enlisted an architect for advice. Which two capabilities of an Identity Provider should the architect detail to help strengthen the business case? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The Identity Provider can store credentials for multiple applications.
optionB: The Identity Provider can authenticate multiple applications.
optionC: The Identity Provider can centralize enterprise password policy.
optionD: The Identity Provider can authenticate multiple social media accounts.
explanation:
The two capabilities worth putting in the business case are that one Identity Provider authenticates users into many applications, and that it centralises enterprise password policy. The first is the single sign-on benefit itself — one login covering the estate rather than one per application. The second is the governance benefit: complexity, expiry, lockout and reset rules are defined once and apply everywhere, instead of drifting apart across each application's own settings.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (stores credentials for multiple applications) — describes a password vault rather than an identity provider. An IdP authenticates the user itself and issues an assertion or token to each application, which is why those applications hold no credentials for it to store.
Option D (authenticates multiple social media accounts) — a genuine capability in consumer scenarios, but a thin argument for an enterprise purchase, and not what a case for centralised employee identity rests on.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) uses Salesforce for Sales Opportunity Management. Okta was recently brought in to Just-in-Time (JIT) provision and authenticate NTO users to applications. Salesforce users also use Okta to authorize a Forecasting web application to access Salesforce records on their behalf. Which two roles are being performed by Salesforce? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: OAuth Resource Server
optionB: SAML Service Provider
optionC: SAML Identity Provider
optionD: OAuth Client
explanation:
Salesforce plays two roles at once here: OAuth Resource Server and SAML Service Provider. Okta authenticates NTO users into Salesforce with SAML, which makes Salesforce the service provider consuming those assertions. Separately, the Forecasting web application calls the Salesforce API with an access token issued on a user's behalf, and the system holding the protected records that token unlocks is the resource server.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (SAML Identity Provider) — that is Okta's role in this scenario. Salesforce consumes the assertion rather than issuing it.
Option D (OAuth Client) — that is the Forecasting application, the party requesting authorization and presenting the token. Salesforce receives the call rather than making it.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/intro_understanding_authentication.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is planning to add Wi-Fi enabled GPS tracking devices to its shipping containers so that the GPS coordinates data can be sent from the tracking device to its Salesforce production org via a custom API. The GPS devices have no direct user input or output capabilities. Which OAuth flow should the identity architect recommend to meet the requirement?
optionA: OAuth 2.0 Web Server Flow for Web App Integration
optionB: OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer Flow for Server-to-Server Integration
optionC: OAuth 2.0 Asset Token Flow for Securing Connected Devices
optionD: OAuth 2.0 Username-Password Flow for Special Scenarios
explanation:
The OAuth 2.0 Asset Token Flow for securing connected devices is the recommendation. It issues a token scoped to the individual device and registers that device as an Asset in Salesforce, giving every tracker a revocable identity of its own — which matters for a fleet of containers, because a shared credential cannot be withdrawn from one lost device without breaking the rest.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Web Server Flow for web app integration) — depends on redirecting a browser and on a user approving access at a login page. The trackers have no direct user input or output, so there is nothing to redirect and nobody to approve.
Option B (JWT Bearer Flow for server-to-server integration) — the closest fit among the distractors, and it would serve one backend integrating on behalf of a known user; but it authorizes a client as a user rather than issuing per-device identity, leaving the whole fleet sharing one certificate and one credential.
Option D (Username-Password Flow) — puts a username and password on every device, offers no per-device revocation, and is the flow Salesforce is retiring for connected apps.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_asset_token_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has an existing Customer Community. UC wants to expand the self-registration capabilities such that customers receive a different community experience based on the data they provide during the registration process. What is the recommended approach an architect should recommend to UC?
optionA: Modify the Community pages to utilize specific fields on the User and Contact records.
optionB: Modify the existing Communities registration controller to assign different profiles.
optionC: Create an after-insert Apex trigger on the User object to assign specific custom permissions.
optionD: Create separate login flows corresponding to the different community user personas.
explanation:
Modifying the Community pages to use specific fields on the User and Contact records is the recommended approach. What the customer supplies at registration is stored on those records, and component visibility and audience targeting in Experience Builder read those values — so a single site renders a different experience per customer with nothing duplicated.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (modify the registration controller to assign different profiles) — a profile controls permissions and access rather than which content a page shows, and splitting customers across profiles to vary an experience multiplies the configuration to maintain.
Option C (an after-insert Apex trigger on User assigning custom permissions) — the same problem with more code, and it runs once at creation, so the experience cannot follow data the customer changes later.
Option D (separate login flows per community persona) — a login flow runs at login and shapes the sign-in sequence; it does not decide what the community pages look like once the user is inside.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_self_registration_configure.htm&type=5&language=en_US
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=experience.community_builder_page_visibilty_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An organization has a central cloud-based Identity and Access Management (IAM) Service for authentication and user management, which must be utilized by all applications as follows: (1) Change of a user status in the central IAM Service triggers provisioning or deprovisioning in the integrated cloud applications; (2) SAML SSO is used to facilitate access for users authenticated at the identity provider (Central IAM Service). Which approach should an IAM architect implement on Salesforce Sales Cloud to meet the requirements?
optionA: Configure central IAM Service as an authentication provider and extend registration handler to manage provisioning and deprovisioning of users.
optionB: Configure Salesforce as a SAML service provider, and enable Just-in-Time (JIT) provisioning and deprovisioning of users.
optionC: Deploy Identity Connect component and set up automated provisioning and deprovisioning of users, as well as SAML-based SSO.
optionD: Configure Salesforce as a SAML Service Provider, and enable SCIM (System for Cross-Domain Identity Management) for provisioning and deprovisioning of users.
explanation:
Salesforce configured as a SAML Service Provider with SCIM enabled meets both requirements. SAML covers the second one, letting users authenticated at the central IAM service reach Salesforce. SCIM covers the first: it gives that service a standard endpoint to push create, update and disable against, so a status change there propagates to Salesforce without anyone having to log in.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an authentication provider with an extended registration handler) — an authentication provider is for OpenID Connect or custom OAuth logins rather than the SAML SSO the requirement specifies, and its registration handler runs at login, so deprovisioning would never fire.
Option B (SAML with Just-in-Time provisioning and deprovisioning) — the near miss. JIT does provision from an assertion, but it runs only when a user logs in, so it cannot deprovision a user whose status change is exactly what stops them logging in.
Option C (Identity Connect) — is built for Microsoft Active Directory on-premises. The source of truth here is a cloud IAM service, which is the case SCIM exists to cover.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_scim_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has a number of employees who do NOT need access to Salesforce objects. The employees should sign in to a custom Benefits web app using their Salesforce credentials. Which license should the identity architect recommend to fulfill this requirement?
optionA: External Identity License
optionB: Identity Only License
optionC: Identity Verification Credits Add-on License
optionD: Identity Connect License
explanation:
The Identity Only License is the one to recommend. It gives an employee Salesforce as their identity — credentials, single sign-on and the App Launcher — so they can sign in to the custom Benefits application with their Salesforce login, while granting no access to Salesforce objects. That is exactly the boundary the requirement draws.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (External Identity License) — the equivalent license for external users such as customers and partners. The people here are NTO's own employees.
Option C (Identity Verification Credits Add-on License) — not an access license at all. It buys the credits consumed when verification methods such as SMS are used.
Option D (Identity Connect License) — not a user license either. Identity Connect is the component that synchronises users from Active Directory into Salesforce.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_licenses.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A global company is using the Salesforce Platform as an Identity Provider and needs to integrate a third-party application with its Experience Cloud customer portal. Which two features should be utilized to provide users with login and identity services for the third-party application? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use the App Launcher with single sign-on (SSO).
optionB: Use Delegated Authentication.
optionC: Use a Connected App.
optionD: External Data Source with Named Principal identity type.
explanation:
A Connected App plus the App Launcher with single sign-on is the pair to use. The connected app registers the third-party application and holds the SAML or OpenID Connect configuration that lets Salesforce assert identity to it; the App Launcher then puts it in front of portal users as a tile they reach without logging in again.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Delegated Authentication) — points the other way: Salesforce calls out to an external web service to verify a password. Here Salesforce is the identity provider, not a system asking someone else to check credentials.
Option D (an External Data Source with a Named Principal identity type) — surfaces external data inside Salesforce, and a named principal means every user shares one integration account. It is a data-access mechanism, not a login and identity service.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_saml_sso.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Identity and Access Management (IAM) Architect is recommending Identity Connect to integrate Microsoft Active Directory (AD) with Salesforce for user provisioning, deprovisioning and single sign-on (SSO). Which feature of Identity Connect is applicable for this scenario?
optionA: If the number of provisioned users exceeds Salesforce license allowances, Identity Connect will start disabling existing Salesforce users in First-In, First-Out (FIFO) fashion.
optionB: Identity Connect can be deployed as a managed package on a Salesforce org, leveraging High Availability of the Salesforce Platform out-of-the-box.
optionC: When configured, Identity Connect acts as an identity provider to both Active Directory and Salesforce, thus providing SSO as a default feature.
optionD: When Identity Connect is in place, if a user is deprovisioned in an on-premise AD, the user's Salesforce session is revoked immediately.
explanation:
Identity Connect synchronises Active Directory into Salesforce in near real time, so when a user is deprovisioned in the on-premises directory the matching Salesforce user is deactivated and their session revoked immediately. That is the feature applicable here: it closes the window between someone leaving and losing access.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (disabling existing users FIFO when provisioned users exceed license allowances) — invents a behaviour. Identity Connect does not deactivate existing users to make room; exceeding the license count is an error to resolve, not something it resolves by choosing victims.
Option B (deployed as a managed package on a Salesforce org, inheriting platform high availability) — Identity Connect is on-premises software installed on a local server, so its availability is the customer's to arrange rather than the platform's.
Option C (acts as an identity provider to both Active Directory and Salesforce) — reverses the relationship. Active Directory remains the identity store; Identity Connect reads from it and translates changes into Salesforce, and it authenticates nobody to AD.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identityconnect_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) wants to improve its engagement with existing customers to boost customer loyalty. To get a better understanding of its customers, NTO establishes a single customer view including their buying behaviors, channel preferences, and purchasing history. All of this information exists but is spread across different systems and formats. NTO has decided to use Salesforce as the platform to build a 360-degree view. The company already uses Microsoft Active Directory (AD) to manage its users and company assets. What should an identity architect do to provision, deprovision, and authenticate users?
optionA: Salesforce Identity can be included but NTO will require Identity Connect.
optionB: Salesforce Identity can be included but NTO will be required to build a custom integration with Microsoft AD.
optionC: Salesforce Identity is not needed since NTO uses Microsoft AD.
optionD: Salesforce Identity is included in the Salesforce licenses so it does not need to be considered separately.
explanation:
Salesforce Identity can be part of this, but with Active Directory already managing users and company assets, NTO will require Identity Connect to bridge the two. It is the supported product for provisioning, deprovisioning and authenticating Salesforce users out of AD, and it does so by configuration rather than code.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (build a custom integration with Microsoft AD) — arrives at the same place by writing and maintaining what Salesforce already ships as a product.
Option C (Salesforce Identity is not needed since NTO uses Microsoft AD) — AD manages the corporate directory but does not provision or authenticate Salesforce users by itself; something has to connect the two.
Option D (Salesforce Identity is included in the licenses, so it needs no separate consideration) — conflates having identity features with having the AD integration. The connection to an on-premises directory is a separate component to plan, license and deploy.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identityconnect_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers uses Salesforce as an identity provider and Concur as the Employee Expense Management system. The HR director wants to ensure Concur accounts for employees are created only after the appropriate approval in the Salesforce org. Which three steps should the identity architect use to implement this requirement? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Enable User Provisioning for the Connected App.
optionB: Create a Connected App for Concur in Salesforce.
optionC: Create an approval process for the UserProvisioningRequest object associated with the provisioning flow.
optionD: Create an approval process for a custom object associated with the provisioning flow.
optionE: Create an approval process for the User object associated with the provisioning flow.
explanation:
The three steps are to create a Connected App for Concur, enable User Provisioning on it, and put an approval process on the UserProvisioningRequest object in the provisioning flow. The connected app represents Concur to Salesforce; User Provisioning is what pushes account lifecycle events to it; and each of those pushes is created as a UserProvisioningRequest record, which is therefore the object an approval can hold until HR has signed off.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option D (an approval process on a custom object associated with the flow) — nothing in the provisioning flow creates or reads a custom object, so an approval there would gate nothing. User Provisioning already supplies a standard object built for this.
Option E (an approval process on the User object) — approves the Salesforce user rather than the Concur account, and the requirement is that the Concur account waits. It would also stall Salesforce user creation, which nobody asked for.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_user_provisioning.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has implemented SAML-based Single Sign-On to provide seamless access to its Salesforce Orgs, financial system, and CPQ system, with PingFederate fronting the SSO and one Salesforce Org also acting as an IdP for other systems. What role combination is represented by the systems in this scenario?
optionA: Salesforce Org1 and Salesforce Org2 are the only Service Providers.
optionB: Salesforce Org1 and PingFederate are acting as Identity Providers.
optionC: Financial System and CPQ System are the only Service Providers.
optionD: Salesforce Org1 and Salesforce Org2 are acting as Identity Providers.
explanation:
Salesforce Org1 and PingFederate are both acting as Identity Providers. This is a hub-and-spoke layout: PingFederate is the corporate IdP fronting the SSO, and one Salesforce org is additionally configured as an IdP for downstream systems. A single system can hold different roles in different SSO chains, which is what makes two identity providers coexist here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Org1 and Org2 are the only Service Providers) — wrong on 'only', and wrong about Org1. The financial and CPQ systems are service providers too, and Org1 is issuing assertions rather than merely consuming them.
Option C (the Financial System and CPQ System are the only Service Providers) — again true as far as it goes and wrong on 'only'. A Salesforce org that consumes an assertion from PingFederate is a service provider in that exchange.
Option D (Org1 and Org2 are acting as Identity Providers) — promotes the wrong second party. It is PingFederate, not the other Salesforce org, that fronts the SSO.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_sfdc_both_sp_idp.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a Customer Community that uses Facebook for authentication. UC would like to ensure that changes in the Facebook profile are reflected on the appropriate Customer Community user. How can this requirement be met?
optionA: Develop a scheduled job that calls out to Facebook on a nightly basis.
optionB: Use SAML Just-in-Time provisioning between Facebook and Salesforce.
optionC: Use information in the signed request that is received from Facebook.
optionD: Use the updateUser() method on the Registration Handler class.
explanation:
The updateUser() method on the Registration Handler class is where this belongs. An Auth Provider's Apex registration handler implements createUser() for the first login and updateUser() for every login after it, and updateUser() receives the current attributes from Facebook each time — so writing them onto the community user there keeps the Salesforce record in step with the Facebook profile.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a nightly scheduled callout to Facebook) — polls for changes Salesforce is already told about at login, adds a day of staleness, and needs an access token per user to make the call.
Option B (SAML Just-in-Time provisioning between Facebook and Salesforce) — Facebook is not a SAML identity provider. Social sign-on runs through an Auth Provider and its registration handler, which is where JIT-style behaviour actually lives here.
Option C (information in the signed request received from Facebook) — a signed request is the Canvas mechanism for passing context into an embedded app, not part of the social sign-on exchange.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_create_registration_handler.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/mobile-sdk/guide/communities-customize-auth-provider.html

question: An architect needs to advise the team that manages the identity provider how to differentiate Salesforce from other service providers. What SAML SSO setting in Salesforce provides this capability?
optionA: Entity ID
optionB: Issuer
optionC: SAML Identity Location
optionD: Identity Provider Login URL
explanation:
The Entity ID is the setting that differentiates Salesforce from other service providers. It is the unique identifier Salesforce presents to the identity provider, and the IdP uses it to look up which service provider configuration — certificate, assertion consumer service URL, attribute mapping — applies to a given request or response. Two Salesforce orgs pointed at the same IdP must carry distinct Entity IDs for this reason.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Issuer) — identifies the identity provider, not Salesforce. It is the value Salesforce checks on an incoming assertion to confirm who sent it, so it differentiates the IdP rather than the SP.
Option C (SAML Identity Location) — says where in the assertion the user's identifier is found, in the Subject or in an attribute element. It concerns identifying the user, not the service provider.
Option D (Identity Provider Login URL) — the endpoint Salesforce sends users to for authentication. It tells Salesforce where to go, and carries nothing that lets the IdP tell one service provider from another.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_saml_sso.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What item should an architect consider when designing a Delegated Authentication implementation?
optionA: The web service should use the Salesforce Federation ID to identify the user.
optionB: The web service should be secured with TLS using Salesforce trusted certificates.
optionC: The web service should be able to accept one to four input method parameters.
optionD: The web service should implement a custom password decryption method.
explanation:
The web service must be secured with TLS using a certificate from a Certificate Authority Salesforce trusts. Delegated Authentication works by Salesforce calling out to an external SOAP service on every login attempt, passing the credentials the user just typed — so the transport is carrying a plaintext password, and anything less than a properly trusted TLS connection exposes it in transit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the service should use the Salesforce Federation ID to identify the user) — the delegated authentication request sends the username the user entered, and it is up to the service to match that against its own directory. Federation ID is a SAML concept and is not what the endpoint receives.
Option C (the service should accept one to four input method parameters) — the signature is fixed, not variable. The WSDL Salesforce publishes for Delegated Authentication defines exactly three inputs: username, password and sourceIp.
Option D (the service should implement a custom password decryption method) — there is nothing to decrypt. The password arrives as submitted, protected by the TLS channel rather than by an application-level encryption scheme.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication_tips.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Salesforce customer is implementing Sales Cloud and a custom pricing application for its call center agents. An Enterprise single sign-on solution is used to authenticate and sign-in users to all applications. The customer has the following requirements: (1) The development team has decided to use a Canvas app to expose the pricing application to agents; (2) Agents should be able to access the Canvas app without needing to log in to the pricing application. Which two options should the identity architect consider to provide support for the Canvas app to initiate login for users? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Configure the Canvas app as a Connected App and set Admin-approved users as pre-authorized.
optionB: Enable SAML in the Connected App and set the SAML Initiation Method as Service Provider Initiated.
optionC: Enable OAuth settings in the Connected App with required OAuth scopes for the pricing application.
optionD: Select 'Enable as a Canvas Personal App' in the Connected App settings.
explanation:
Two settings on the Connected App carry this. Marking the Canvas app's permitted users as 'Admin-approved users are pre-authorized' means the agent is never shown an approval screen — access is decided by profile and permission set assignment in advance. Enabling SAML on the same connected app with the SAML Initiation Method set to Service Provider Initiated makes Salesforce the identity provider that signs the agent in to the pricing application when the canvas loads, which is what removes the second login.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (enable OAuth settings with the scopes the pricing application needs) — OAuth is the alternative Canvas authentication model, and it would put an authorization step in front of the user rather than signing them in from the enterprise SSO session already established.
Option D (select 'Enable as a Canvas Personal App') — lets individual users install the canvas app for themselves. That is a distribution choice and it does nothing to initiate login, besides pulling against the admin-approved model in option A.
References:
