https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_connect.meta/platform_connect/canvas_framework_intro.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_connect.meta/platform_connect/canvas_app_saml_sso_intro.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.connected_app_manage_oauth.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An architect needs to set up a Facebook Authentication Provider as a login option for a Salesforce Customer Community. What portion of the authentication provider setup associates a Facebook user with a Salesforce user?
optionA: Consumer Key and Consumer Secret
optionB: Apex Registration Handler
optionC: User Info Endpoint URL
optionD: Federation ID
explanation:
The Apex Registration Handler is the part that associates a Facebook user with a Salesforce user. It receives the profile data returned by Facebook and decides what to do with it — create a new community user, or link the identity to an existing one — and that decision, persisted as a third-party account link, is the association the question asks about.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Consumer Key and Consumer Secret) — identify the Salesforce application to Facebook so the OAuth exchange can happen at all. They authenticate the app, not the person.
Option C (User Info Endpoint URL) — is where the provider's profile attributes are fetched from. It supplies the raw material the handler works with, but performs no matching itself.
Option D (Federation ID) — a field used to match a user in SAML single sign-on. Social sign-on through an Auth Provider matches through the registration handler instead.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_create_registration_handler.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/mobile-sdk/guide/communities-customize-auth-provider.html

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing Salesforce and would like to establish SAML SSO for its users to log in. UC stores its corporate user identities in a custom database. The UC IT manager has heard good things about Salesforce Identity Connect as an IdP and would like to understand what limitations they may face if they decided to use Identity Connect in their current environment. What limitation should an architect inform the IT manager about?
optionA: Identity Connect is not compatible with UC's current identity environment.
optionB: Identity Connect will only support IdP-initiated SAML flows in UC's current environment.
optionC: Identity Connect will only support SP-initiated SAML flows in UC's current environment.
optionD: Identity Connect will not support user provisioning in UC's current environment.
explanation:
Identity Connect is not compatible with UC's current identity environment, and that is the limitation to raise. Identity Connect integrates Microsoft Active Directory with Salesforce; UC's corporate identities live in a custom database, so there is nothing for it to synchronise against. UC would need a SAML identity provider capable of authenticating against that database instead.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (it will only support IdP-initiated SAML flows here) — presumes Identity Connect works in this environment and is merely restricted. It does not work here at all, and the limitation is not about flow direction.
Option C (it will only support SP-initiated SAML flows here) — the same presumption with the direction reversed, and wrong for the same reason.
Option D (it will not support user provisioning here) — names a real Identity Connect capability and denies just that one. The problem is broader: without Active Directory, neither provisioning nor authentication is available.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identityconnect_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is building a customer community and will allow customers to authenticate using Facebook credentials. The first time the user authenticates using Facebook, UC would like a customer account created automatically in their accounting system. The accounting system has a web service accessible to Salesforce for the creation of accounts. How can the architect meet these requirements?
optionA: Create a custom application on Heroku that manages the sign-on process from Facebook.
optionB: Use JIT provisioning to automatically create the account in the accounting system.
optionC: Use OAuth JWT flow to pass the data from Salesforce to the accounting system.
optionD: Add an Apex callout in the Registration Handler of the Authorization Provider.
explanation:
Adding an Apex callout in the Registration Handler of the Authorization Provider is how this is met. The handler's createUser() method runs the first time someone authenticates through Facebook, which is exactly the moment the requirement names, and an Apex callout from there can invoke the accounting system's web service so the customer account is created alongside the community user.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom application on Heroku managing the sign-on process) — replaces a supported Auth Provider with an application to build, host and maintain, and inserts an extra system into the login path for no gain.
Option B (JIT provisioning to create the account in the accounting system) — Just-in-Time provisioning creates users in Salesforce from an incoming SAML assertion. It does not push records into a third-party system, and Facebook is not a SAML identity provider.
Option C (the OAuth JWT flow to pass data to the accounting system) — describes how a client authenticates to Salesforce, not how Salesforce sends data outward, and it supplies no hook tied to a customer's first login.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_create_registration_handler.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/mobile-sdk/guide/communities-customize-auth-provider.html

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a classified information system that its call center team uses only when they are working on a case with a record type 'Classified'. They are only allowed to access the system when they own an open 'Classified' case, and their access to the system is removed at all other times. They would like to implement SAML SSO with Salesforce as the IdP, and automatically allow or deny the staff's access to the classified information system based on whether they currently own an open 'Classified' case record, when they try to access the system using SSO. What is the recommended solution for automatically allowing or denying access to the classified information system based on the open 'Classified' case record criteria?
optionA: Use Custom SAML JIT Provisioning to dynamically query the user's open 'Classified' cases when attempting to access the classified information system.
optionB: Use Apex trigger on Case to dynamically assign permission sets that grant access when a user is assigned an open 'Classified' case, and remove it when the case is closed.
optionC: Use Salesforce reports to identify users that currently own open 'Classified' cases and should be granted access to the classified information system.
optionD: Use a custom Connected App Handler using Apex to dynamically allow access to the system based on whether the staff owns any open 'Classified' cases.
explanation:
A custom Connected App Handler in Apex is the recommended solution. A class extending ConnectedAppPlugin runs as part of each SSO attempt into the connected app, so it can query at that moment whether the user owns an open 'Classified' case and allow or deny the login accordingly. Evaluating the rule at the point of access is what makes access appear and disappear with the case, which is the requirement.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom SAML JIT provisioning querying the user's open cases) — JIT provisioning runs on the service provider side, creating or updating a user from an incoming assertion. Salesforce is the identity provider here, so JIT is on the wrong side of the exchange.
Option B (an Apex trigger on Case assigning and removing permission sets) — the closest workable alternative, and still second best: it maintains a standing grant that has to be kept correct through reassignment, reopening and multiple cases, and it grants access between case events rather than deciding at the moment of access.
Option C (Salesforce reports identifying users who own open cases) — produces a list for a person to act on. Nothing about it is automatic, and access would lag the case by however long the manual step takes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_class_Auth_ConnectedAppPlugin.htm

question: Universal Containers wants to build a custom mobile app connecting to Salesforce using OAuth, and would like to restrict the types of resources mobile users can access. What OAuth feature of Salesforce should be used to achieve the goal?
optionA: Access Tokens
optionB: Scopes
optionC: Mobile PINs
optionD: Refresh Tokens
explanation:
Scopes are the OAuth feature that restricts what mobile users can reach. A scope is requested at authorization time and fixes what the resulting access token may do — api, web, refresh_token, openid and the rest — so limiting the scopes the Connected App allows limits the resources the app can touch, whatever the user's own permissions would otherwise permit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Access Tokens) — the credential whose privileges are being limited, not the mechanism that limits them. A token carries whatever the granted scopes allowed.
Option C (Mobile PINs) — a device-level protection requiring a PIN to unlock the app. It controls who is holding the phone, not which resources the app may call.
Option D (Refresh Tokens) — governs how long access lasts without re-authentication. It affects duration, not the set of resources reachable.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An identity architect is implementing a mobile-first Consumer Identity Access Management (CIAM) for external users. User authentication is the only requirement. The user's email or mobile phone number should be supported as a username. Which two licenses are needed to meet this requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: External Identity Licenses
optionB: Identity Connect Licenses
optionC: SMS Verification Credits
optionD: Email Verification Credits
explanation:
Two licenses are needed: External Identity Licenses and SMS Verification Credits. External Identity is the license type for external users who need authentication and nothing more, which is the whole requirement here. SMS Verification Credits are what a mobile-first design consumes: supporting a mobile phone number as the username means one-time passcodes delivered by text, and each of those messages spends a credit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Identity Connect Licenses) — Identity Connect synchronises users from Microsoft Active Directory into Salesforce. There is no corporate directory in a consumer CIAM scenario for it to read.
Option D (Email Verification Credits) — no such license exists. Delivering a verification code by email consumes nothing, which is precisely why only the SMS side has to be bought.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_sms_identity_verification.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_licenses.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005239145&language=en_US&type=1

question: An identity architect wants to secure Salesforce APIs using Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML). For security purposes, administrators will need to authorize the applications that will be consuming the APIs. Which Salesforce OAuth authorization flow should be used?
optionA: OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow
optionB: SAML Assertion Flow
optionC: OAuth 2.0 User-Agent Flow
optionD: OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer Flow
explanation:
The OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow is the one to use. Salesforce titles its documentation for this flow 'for Previously Authorized Apps', and its first setup step is to create a connected app and register an X509 certificate against it. That connected app is the record an administrator authorizes, so only approved client applications can exchange a SAML assertion for an access token — which is exactly the control the requirement asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (SAML Assertion Flow) — Salesforce documents this separately from the flow above, and it is the near miss here. What selects the keyed answer is the administrator-authorization requirement in the stem, which the SAML Bearer Assertion Flow delivers through the connected app and its registered certificate.
Option C (OAuth 2.0 User-Agent Flow) — redirects a browser so an end user can approve access interactively. It secures nothing with SAML and puts the authorization decision with the user rather than an administrator.
Option D (OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer Flow) — the same shape of answer built on a JSON Web Token rather than a SAML assertion. It is the right choice when the trust is expressed as a JWT; the requirement here specifies SAML.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_SAML_bearer_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses Salesforce to allow customers to keep track of the order status. The customers can log in to Salesforce using external authentication providers, such as Facebook and Google. UC is also leveraging the App Launcher to let customers access an off-platform application for generating shipping labels. The label generator application uses OAuth to provide users access. What license type should an architect recommend for the customers?
optionA: External Identity License
optionB: Identity License
optionC: Customer Community Plus License
optionD: Customer Community License
explanation:
The External Identity License is the one to recommend. These are customers, not employees, and what they need is authentication — logging in through Facebook or Google — plus the App Launcher and OAuth-based single sign-on into the off-platform label generator. External Identity covers exactly that set without granting the CRM record access a community license pays for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Identity License) — the equivalent license for internal employees. The users here are UC's customers.
Option C (Customer Community Plus License) — adds roles, sharing and delegated administration for external users who work with Salesforce records. Nothing in the scenario needs it, and it costs more.
Option D (Customer Community License) — also aimed at customers working with records such as cases and accounts. Tracking order status through login and SSO does not require it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_licenses.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers would like its customers to register and log in to a portal built on Salesforce Experience Cloud. Customers should be able to use their Facebook or LinkedIn credentials for ease of use. Which three steps should an identity architect take to implement social sign-on? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Create authentication providers for both Facebook and LinkedIn.
optionB: Check 'Facebook' and 'LinkedIn' under Login Page Setup.
optionC: Enable 'Federated Single Sign-On Using SAML'.
optionD: Update the default registration handlers to create and update users.
optionE: Register both Facebook and LinkedIn as Connected Apps.
explanation:
Three steps implement social sign-on. Create authentication providers for Facebook and LinkedIn — Salesforce ships predefined provider types for both. Check Facebook and LinkedIn under the site's Login Page Setup, which is what puts the social buttons on the login page. Then update the default registration handlers so the attributes each provider returns are used to create and update community users.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (enable 'Federated Single Sign-On Using SAML') — social sign-on runs over OAuth and OpenID Connect through an Auth Provider. Neither Facebook nor LinkedIn is being used as a SAML identity provider here.
Option E (register Facebook and LinkedIn as Connected Apps) — points outward. A connected app describes an application that Salesforce asserts identity to; here Salesforce is consuming identities those providers assert, which is what an Auth Provider is for.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_authentication_providers.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_create_registration_handler.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) plans to use a SAML-based third-party IdP serving both the Salesforce Partner Community and the corporate portal. UC partners will log in to the corporate portal to access protected resources, including links to Salesforce resources. What would be the recommended way to configure the IdP so that seamless access can be achieved in this scenario?
optionA: Set up the corporate portal as a Connected App in Salesforce and use the Web Server OAuth flow.
optionB: Configure SP-initiated SSO that passes the SAML token upon Salesforce resource access request.
optionC: Set up the corporate portal as a Connected App in Salesforce and use the User Agent OAuth flow.
optionD: Configure IdP-initiated SSO that passes the SAML token upon Salesforce resource access request.
explanation:
IdP-initiated SSO is the recommended configuration. The partner has already authenticated at the corporate portal through the shared identity provider, so a link to a Salesforce resource should carry that existing session across: the IdP posts a SAML assertion straight to Salesforce's assertion consumer service, and the user lands on the resource in one hop with no Salesforce login page in between.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (SP-initiated SSO) — the plausible alternative, and the slower path here. It sends the user to Salesforce first, which then redirects back to the IdP to discover an authentication that has already happened, adding round trips to reach the same place.
Option A (the corporate portal as a Connected App using the Web Server OAuth flow) — OAuth authorizes an application to call APIs on a user's behalf. It does not sign a partner in to the Salesforce user interface, which is what following a link to a Salesforce resource requires.
Option C (the corporate portal as a Connected App using the User Agent OAuth flow) — the same mismatch, with the added exposure of returning a token in the browser. The scenario is SAML SSO between an established IdP and Salesforce.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000315559&language=en_US&type=1

question: A division of Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) purchased Salesforce. NTO uses a third-party identity provider (IdP) to validate user credentials against its corporate Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) directory. NTO wants to help employees remember as few passwords as possible. What should an identity architect recommend?
optionA: Set up Salesforce as a Service Provider to the existing IdP.
optionB: Use Salesforce Connect to synchronize LDAP passwords to Salesforce.
optionC: Set up Salesforce as an IdP to authenticate against the LDAP directory.
optionD: Set up Salesforce as an Authentication Provider to the existing IdP.
explanation:
Setting Salesforce up as a Service Provider to the existing identity provider is the recommendation. The IdP already validates credentials against the corporate LDAP directory, so making Salesforce one more service provider in that federation means employees sign in with the corporate password they already have and gain no new one to remember.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (use Salesforce Connect to synchronise LDAP passwords) — Salesforce Connect surfaces external data as external objects. It is a data-integration feature and moves no credentials; synchronising passwords would also create the second password the requirement is trying to avoid.
Option C (set Salesforce up as an IdP authenticating against the LDAP directory) — Salesforce cannot authenticate against LDAP directly, and it inverts a working arrangement in which the third-party IdP already owns that job.
Option D (set Salesforce up as an Authentication Provider to the existing IdP) — misuses the term. An Auth Provider is configuration inside Salesforce for accepting OpenID Connect or custom OAuth logins; it is not something Salesforce becomes for another identity provider.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to build a custom mobile app for their field reps to create orders in Salesforce. After the first time the users log in, they must be able to access Salesforce upon opening the mobile app without being prompted to log in again. What OAuth flows should be considered to support this requirement?
optionA: Mobile Agent flow with a Bearer Token.
optionB: User-Agent flow with a Refresh Token.
optionC: SAML Assertion flow with a Bearer Token.
optionD: Web Server flow with a Refresh Token.
explanation:
The User-Agent flow with a Refresh Token is the answer this item keys. Requesting the refresh_token scope means the device stores a refresh token after the first login and silently exchanges it for a new access token thereafter, so the field rep is never prompted again.
However, Salesforce now explicitly recommends the Web Server flow with PKCE for native and mobile apps instead of the User-Agent flow. The User-Agent, or implicit, grant delivers the access token in the URL fragment, creating a token-leakage risk through browser history and redirect-URL interception, and administrators can disable the flow entirely at the Connected App level for that reason. The Web Server flow with a refresh token satisfies the same no-re-login requirement while the code exchange happens server-side with a PKCE code verifier. On the current platform that is the architecturally preferred choice for a new mobile implementation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Mobile Agent flow with a Bearer Token) — there is no such OAuth flow. The name blends the user-agent flow with bearer-token terminology.
Option C (SAML Assertion flow with a Bearer Token) — requires an existing SAML assertion from an identity provider that has already authenticated the user. Field reps opening a custom app are not arriving from a SAML IdP, and the flow issues no refresh token to keep them signed in.
Option D (Web Server flow with a Refresh Token) — meets the stated requirement as well, and is the flow Salesforce now recommends for mobile, as set out above. It is not what this item keys, which reflects the legacy exam answer; weigh the paragraph above before carrying B into a real design.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.remoteaccess_oauth_user_agent_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_web_server_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has a requirement to ensure all user logins include a single multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompt. Currently, users are allowed the choice to login with a username and password or via single sign-on against NTO's corporate Identity Provider, which includes built-in MFA. Which configuration will meet this requirement?
optionA: Create and assign a permission set to all employees that includes 'MFA for User Interface Logins.'
optionB: Enable 'MFA for User Interface Logins' for your organization from Setup -> Identity Verification.
optionC: For all employee profiles, set the Session Level Required at Login to High Assurance and add the corporate identity provider to the High Assurance list for the org's Session Security Levels.
optionD: Create a custom login flow that enforces MFA and assign it to a permission set. Then assign the permission set to all employees.
explanation:
The requirement has two login paths and asks for exactly one MFA prompt on each. Session security levels are the documented way to get that, and Salesforce spells out both halves.
On the profile side: 'For Session Security Level Required at Login, select High Assurance to require users to verify their identity with multi-factor authentication when they log in.' That guarantees a prompt for anyone logging in directly with a username and password.
On the org side, the Session Settings page is where an SSO provider's own MFA is recognised: 'If users access Salesforce via single sign-on (SSO) only and you're using your SSO provider's MFA solution: Put your SSO provider in the High Assurance column.' A user arriving through NTO's corporate IdP therefore lands in a high-assurance session already, satisfying the login requirement without a second Salesforce challenge. Together these produce one prompt per path, which is what the stem asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a permission set granting 'MFA for User Interface Logins' to all employees) — forces Salesforce's own challenge on every UI login, including users who have already completed MFA at the identity provider. That is the double prompt the requirement rules out.
Option B (enabling 'MFA for User Interface Logins' org-wide from Identity Verification) — the same double prompt, applied from the org rather than a permission set. Salesforce does not infer trust from a SAML authentication context here; the documented way to honour an IdP's MFA is the High Assurance column.
Option D (a custom login flow enforcing MFA, assigned by permission set) — builds by hand what session security levels already provide, and a flow that challenges everyone reintroduces the second prompt for SSO users unless it re-implements the branching the platform does declaratively.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.understand_mfa_high_assurance_login_session.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_session.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer moved B->C. The old explanation defended the org-wide MFA setting by asserting that 'Salesforce intelligently honors the IdP's MFA when the SAML assertion advertises an authn context, avoiding double prompts.' No documentation supports that mechanism, and the article written for this exact problem prescribes a different one: put the SSO provider in the High Assurance column of Session Settings so SSO users arrive with a high-assurance session, and require High Assurance at login so direct logins are challenged once. That is option C, both halves quotable. Option B would double-prompt precisely the SSO population whose IdP already enforces MFA, which is what the single-prompt requirement forbids.

question: IT security at Universal Containers (UC) is concerned about recent phishing scams targeting its users and wants to add additional layers of login protection. What should an architect recommend to address the issue?
optionA: Use the Salesforce Authenticator mobile app with two-step verification.
optionB: Implement Single Sign-On using a corporate identity store.
optionC: Lock sessions to the IP address from which they originated.
optionD: Increase Password complexity requirements in Salesforce.
explanation:
Salesforce Authenticator with two-step verification is the recommendation. Phishing harvests passwords, and a second factor is what makes a harvested password insufficient on its own. The push-based approval also puts the login's location and IP in front of the user before they approve, so an attempt from somewhere they are not is visible rather than silent.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (single sign-on against a corporate identity store) — moves the password to a different login page rather than adding a layer. Unless that identity provider enforces MFA of its own, a phished corporate credential works just as well.
Option C (lock sessions to their originating IP address) — protects a session already established against hijacking mid-flight. It does nothing about an attacker who has the password and simply starts their own session.
Option D (increase password complexity requirements) — raises the cost of guessing a password, which is not how phishing works. A complex password handed over on a fake login page is as useful to the attacker as a simple one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_require_two_factor_authentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_overview_2fa.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to integrate a third-party reward calculation system with Salesforce to calculate rewards. Rewards will be calculated on a scheduled basis and updated back into Salesforce. The integration between Salesforce and the reward calculation system needs to be secure. Which are two recommended practices for using OAuth flow in this scenario? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: OAuth Refresh Token Flow
optionB: OAuth JWT Bearer Token Flow
optionC: OAuth SAML Bearer Assertion Flow
optionD: OAuth Username-Password Flow
explanation:
The JWT Bearer Token Flow and the SAML Bearer Assertion Flow are the two recommended practices. Both authorize a server-to-server integration by presenting a signed assertion — a JWT signed with a certificate's private key, or a signed SAML assertion — so the reward calculation system proves who it is on a schedule, unattended, without storing anyone's password.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Refresh Token Flow) — a refresh token only exists after a user has completed an interactive flow and approved access. A scheduled batch integration has no user at the keyboard to produce one.
Option D (Username-Password Flow) — puts a real username and password in the integration's configuration and sends them on every exchange. Salesforce is retiring it for connected apps, and it is the option a security requirement rules out first.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_jwt_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_SAML_bearer_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has decided to implement a federated single sign-on solution using a third-party IdP. In reviewing the third-party products, they would like to ensure the product supports the automated provisioning and deprovisioning of users. What are the underlying mechanisms that the UC architect must ensure are part of the product?
optionA: Just-in-Time (JIT) for Provisioning; SOAP API for Deprovisioning.
optionB: Just-in-Time (JIT) for both Provisioning and Deprovisioning.
optionC: Provisioning API for both Provisioning and Deprovisioning.
optionD: SOAP API for Provisioning; Just-in-Time (JIT) for Deprovisioning.
explanation:
The product must supply Just-in-Time provisioning for provisioning and an API call for deprovisioning. JIT creates or updates the Salesforce user from the SAML assertion when the user successfully authenticates, which covers provisioning at first login. It cannot cover deprovisioning, because deprovisioning means the user can no longer authenticate — so the JIT handler never fires and something has to reach into Salesforce explicitly to deactivate the record.
SCIM is the modern standard for that deprovisioning call, but this option set offers the SOAP API, and both are valid mechanisms for it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (JIT for both provisioning and deprovisioning) — the common misreading. JIT is driven by a successful authentication, so it can never initiate the one action that follows a user losing the ability to authenticate.
Option C (a provisioning API for both) — would work for deprovisioning, but discards JIT for the case it exists to serve, replacing an automatic first-login provision with an integration to build.
Option D (SOAP API for provisioning, JIT for deprovisioning) — has both halves the wrong way round, and asks JIT to do the one thing it structurally cannot.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_calls_create.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_scim_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses a home-grown employee portal for their employees to collaborate. UC decides to use Salesforce Ideas to allow the employees to post ideas from the employee portal. When clicking some links in the employee portal, the users should be redirected to Salesforce, authenticated, and presented with relevant pages. What scope should be requested when using the OAuth token to meet this requirement?
optionA: Web
optionB: API
optionC: Visualforce
optionD: Full
explanation:
The web scope is the one to request. It lets the access token be exchanged for a Salesforce user-interface session through frontdoor.jsp, so a user clicking a link in the employee portal is redirected into Salesforce, authenticated, and dropped on the relevant Ideas page — which is exactly the behaviour described.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (api) — grants access to the REST and SOAP APIs. It lets a program read and write data, but it will not land a person inside the Salesforce user interface.
Option C (Visualforce) — allows access to Visualforce pages, which is narrower than the requirement and does not itself establish the UI session that the redirect depends on.
Option D (full) — would technically work, since it includes web, but it grants every permission the user has to the token. Requesting the one scope the job needs is the practice to recommend.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has an e-commerce website where customers can buy products, make payments, and manage their accounts. UC decides to build a Customer Community on Salesforce and wants to allow the customers to access the community for their accounts without logging in again. UC decides to implement an SP-initiated SSO using a SAML-based compliant IdP. In this scenario where Salesforce is the Service Provider, which two activities must be performed in Salesforce to make SP-initiated SSO work? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Configure Delegated Authentication.
optionB: Create a Connected App.
optionC: Configure SAML SSO settings.
optionD: Set up My Domain.
explanation:
Two things must be configured in Salesforce: the SAML SSO settings and My Domain. The SAML settings are where the identity provider's certificate, Issuer, Entity ID and assertion consumer service URL are registered so Salesforce can validate an incoming assertion. My Domain is what makes SP-initiated SSO possible at all, because Salesforce needs a unique org URL from which to issue the AuthnRequest — without it the request would start at a hostname shared by every org.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (configure Delegated Authentication) — a different mechanism entirely, in which Salesforce calls an external SOAP service to verify a password. It is not part of a SAML exchange.
Option B (create a Connected App) — is what you build when Salesforce is the identity provider asserting outward to another application. Here Salesforce is the service provider consuming an assertion, so no connected app is involved.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.domain_name_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000315559&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_service_provider_configuration.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A real estate company wants to provide its customers a digital space to design their interior decoration options. To simplify the registration to gain access to the community site (built in Experience Cloud), the CTO has requested that the IT/Development team provide the option for customers to use their existing social-media credentials to register and access. The IT lead has approached the Salesforce Identity and Access Management (IAM) architect for technical direction on implementing the social sign-on (for Facebook, Twitter, and a new provider that supports standard OpenID Connect (OIDC)). Which two recommendations should the Salesforce IAM architect make to the IT Lead? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Authentication provider configuration is required for each social sign-on provider; and enable Authentication Providers in the community.
optionB: Use a declarative registration handler process builder/flow to create, update users and contacts.
optionC: Apex coding skills are needed for the Registration Handler to create and update users.
optionD: For supporting OIDC, it is necessary to enable SAML with Just-in-Time provisioning (JIT) and OAuth 2.0.
explanation:
Two things are genuinely required for social sign-on. Each provider needs its own authentication provider configured — Facebook, Twitter, and the OIDC provider alike, since Salesforce supports 'OpenID Connect or... a custom OAuth 2.0 configuration' — and those providers must then be enabled on the site's login page before the social buttons appear. That is option A.
The second requirement is a registration handler, which is mandatory rather than optional: 'To set up single sign-on (SSO) with an authentication provider, you must set up a registration handler.' Its job is to take the attributes the social provider returns, look for a matching user, and create or update accordingly.
One important currency note. Apex is a supported way to write that handler, but it is no longer the only one — Salesforce now states that 'to set up a registration handler, you can use Flow Builder or Apex', and describes the flow option as something that 'can be configured and maintained entirely with clicks instead of code. No developer knowledge is necessary.' So read option C as naming a supported implementation, not an unavoidable prerequisite; a modern build can satisfy this requirement declaratively.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a declarative registration handler built in Process Builder or Flow) — as printed it names Process Builder, which is retired and was never a way to build a registration handler. Given the currency note above, treat this option as dated rather than as a clean falsehood: Flow Builder genuinely is a supported alternative to Apex today.
Option D (enable SAML with Just-in-Time provisioning and OAuth 2.0 to support OIDC) — unnecessary. An OpenID Connect provider is handled natively by the authentication provider framework, with no SAML configuration or JIT provisioning bolted on beside it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_create_registration_handler.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_authentication_providers.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A,C left in place but the item is now partly stale, and the explanation says so instead of asserting the old absolute. Option C claims 'Apex coding skills are needed for the Registration Handler', which was true when the item was written and is no longer: Salesforce documents Flow Builder as a first-class registration handler type requiring no developer knowledge. That also makes option B closer to true than the deck allowed. I did not move the key to A,B because B's wording names Process Builder, which is retired, so neither option is cleanly correct as printed. Flagged as a judgement call for the user: the cleanest repair is to reword C to 'a registration handler is required (Apex or Flow)' rather than to reletter the key.

question: What information does the 'RelayState' parameter contain in SP-initiated Single Sign-On?
optionA: Reference to the login address URL of the service provider.
optionB: Reference to the login address URL of the identity provider.
optionC: Reference to a URL redirect parameter at the service provider.
optionD: Reference to a URL redirect parameter at the identity provider.
explanation:
RelayState carries a reference to a URL redirect parameter at the service provider. The service provider sets it before redirecting the browser to the identity provider; the IdP treats the value as opaque and echoes it back unchanged with the SAML response; and the SP then uses it to send the user to the page they originally asked for. That is what lets a deep link survive an SSO round trip instead of dumping the user on a home page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the login address URL of the service provider) — the SP's login address is not what RelayState holds; it points at the resource the user wanted, not at the way in.
Option B (the login address URL of the identity provider) — that is the Identity Provider Login URL configured in the SSO settings, a separate value that tells Salesforce where to send users for authentication.
Option D (a URL redirect parameter at the identity provider) — puts the destination on the wrong side. The IdP never interprets RelayState; it hands the value straight back, precisely so the SP can decide where the user lands.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000386068&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers (UC) is building a mobile application that will make calls to the Salesforce REST API. Additionally, UC would like to provide the optimal experience for its mobile users. Which two OAuth scopes should UC configure in the Connected App? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: full
optionB: api
optionC: web
optionD: refresh_token
explanation:
The two scopes are api and refresh_token. The api scope is what lets the mobile application call the Salesforce REST API at all. The refresh_token scope is what delivers the optimal mobile experience: with a refresh token stored on the device, the app renews its access token silently instead of asking the user to sign in again.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (full) — grants every permission the user holds, well beyond calling the REST API, and still would not by itself return a refresh token. It fails least privilege for no benefit.
Option C (web) — exists to exchange a token for a Salesforce user-interface session through frontdoor.jsp. This application is calling the API, not opening Salesforce pages.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is planning to implement a community for its customers using Salesforce Experience Cloud. Customers are not able to self-register. NTO would like to have customers set their own passwords when provided access to the community. Which two recommendations should an identity architect make to fulfill this requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Enable Welcome emails while configuring the Experience Cloud site.
optionB: Allow Password reset using the API to update Experience Cloud site membership.
optionC: Use Login Flows to allow users to reset passwords in Experience Cloud site.
optionD: Add customers as contacts and add them to Experience Cloud site.
explanation:
Two recommendations fulfil this. Add the customers as contacts and enable them as members of the Experience Cloud site — that is the administrator-driven path when self-registration is off, since a community user is created from a contact. Then enable Welcome emails on the site, so each newly created member receives a message with a link to set a password of their own, which is the requirement that customers choose their own.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (allow password reset using the API to update site membership) — conflates two things. The API can create and update members, but a password reset is not how a new user is given first access, and nothing here needs membership updated through code.
Option C (use Login Flows to let users reset passwords) — a login flow runs after a user has authenticated, which a customer who has never had a password cannot do. It is a mechanism for users who are already in.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_create_external_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.faq_communities_external_member_login_info.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator created a Connected App for a custom web application in Salesforce which needs to be visible as a tile in App Launcher. The tile for the custom web application is missing in the App Launcher for all users in Salesforce. The administrator requested assistance from an identity architect to resolve the issue. Which two reasons are the source of the issue? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The Connected App is not set in the App menu as 'Visible in App Launcher'.
optionB: Session Policy is set as 'High Assurance Session required' for this Connected App.
optionC: OAuth scope does not include 'openid'.
optionD: Start URL for the Connected App is not set in Connected App settings.
explanation:
Two settings explain a tile that is missing for everyone. The Connected App must be marked 'Visible in App Launcher' in the App menu — if it is hidden there, no user sees it regardless of their permissions. It must also carry a Start URL, because that is the destination the tile launches to; without one there is nothing for the App Launcher to render as a tile.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a 'High Assurance session required' policy on the Connected App) — governs what happens when a user opens the app, prompting them to raise their session level. It does not remove the tile from the App Launcher.
Option C (the OAuth scope not including openid) — openid is what allows an OpenID Connect identity token to be issued. It affects what the app learns about the user after launch, not whether the tile appears.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000272761&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_saml_sso.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to build a mobile application that will be making calls to the Salesforce REST API. UC's Salesforce implementation relies heavily on custom objects and custom Apex code. UC does not want its users to have to enter credentials every time they use the app. Which two scope values should an architect recommend to UC? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: api
optionB: full
optionC: refresh_token
optionD: custom_permissions
explanation:
The two scopes to recommend are api and refresh_token. The api scope covers the REST API, and it reaches custom objects and Apex REST endpoints alike, so UC's heavy use of custom development needs nothing extra. The refresh_token scope is what stops users re-entering credentials: it issues a long-lived refresh token the app exchanges for new access tokens in the background.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (full) — grants more than the application needs. It would work, which is what makes it tempting, but requesting every permission a user holds to call one API is the opposite of least privilege.
Option D (custom_permissions) — returns the custom permissions the user has been granted, as information. It grants no API access and does nothing to keep the user signed in.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: In a typical SSL setup involving a trusted party and trusting party, what consideration should an architect take into account when using digital certificates?
optionA: Use of self-signed certificate leads to higher maintenance for trusting party because the cert needs to be added to their truststore.
optionB: Use of self-signed certificate leads to lower maintenance for trusted party because multiple self-signed certs need to be maintained.
optionC: Use of self-signed certificate leads to higher maintenance for trusted party because they have to act as the trusted CA.
optionD: Use of self-signed certificate leads to lower maintenance for trusting party because there is no trusted CA cert to maintain.
explanation:
A self-signed certificate raises maintenance for the trusting party, because that specific certificate has to be added to their truststore. There is no certificate authority in the chain to vouch for it, so trust is established per certificate rather than once at the CA root — and every rotation by the trusted party means another update on the trusting side.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (lower maintenance for the trusted party because multiple self-signed certificates need to be maintained) — argues against itself. More certificates to maintain is more work, not less.
Option C (higher maintenance for the trusted party because they have to act as the trusted CA) — puts the burden on the wrong side. Issuing oneself a certificate is trivial; the cost lands on whoever has to decide to trust it.
Option D (lower maintenance for the trusting party because there is no CA certificate to maintain) — inverts the outcome. Trusting one CA root covers every certificate it signs, which is precisely why it is the cheaper arrangement to maintain.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_keys_uploading_mutual_auth_cert_api.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_keys_uploading_mutual_auth_cert.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) employees use a custom on-premise helpdesk application to request, approve, notify, and track access granted to various on-premises and cloud applications, including Salesforce. Salesforce is currently used to authenticate users. How should NTO provision Salesforce users as soon as they are approved in the helpdesk application with the approved profiles and permission sets?
optionA: Use Salesforce Connect to integrate with the helpdesk application.
optionB: Have the helpdesk initiate an IdP-initiated Just-in-Time provisioning SAML flow.
optionC: Build an integration that performs a remote call-in to the Salesforce SOAP or REST API.
optionD: Use a login flow to query the helpdesk to validate user status.
explanation:
An integration that performs a remote call-in to the Salesforce SOAP or REST API is the answer. The helpdesk is the system of record for approvals, and the requirement is that provisioning happens as soon as an approval lands — so the helpdesk pushes the event, creating or updating the User and assigning the approved profile and permission sets at that moment.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce Connect to integrate with the helpdesk) — surfaces external data as external objects for reading and writing. It does not create Salesforce users or assign them permissions.
Option B (an IdP-initiated Just-in-Time provisioning SAML flow) — the closest alternative, and it provisions at the wrong moment. JIT acts when the user next logs in, which may be long after approval, and the stem asks for provisioning as soon as the approval is given.
Option D (a login flow querying the helpdesk to validate user status) — also runs at login, and it checks a user who must already exist in Salesforce to reach it. It validates rather than provisions.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/intro_understanding_authentication.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_scim_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is building a custom Innovation platform on their Salesforce instance. The Innovation platform will be written completely in Apex and Visualforce and will use custom objects to store the data. UC would like all users to be able to access the system without having to log in with Salesforce credentials. UC will utilize a third-party IdP using SAML SSO. What is the optimal Salesforce license type for all of the UC employees?
optionA: Salesforce Platform License.
optionB: External Identity License.
optionC: Salesforce License.
optionD: Identity License.
explanation:
The Salesforce Platform License is the optimal type. The Innovation platform is built entirely from Apex, Visualforce and custom objects, which is exactly the scope a Platform license covers, and it supports SAML single sign-on so employees reach it through the third-party IdP without Salesforce credentials.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (External Identity License) — is for external users such as customers and partners, and grants identity services rather than access to custom application data. These are UC employees using the platform itself.
Option C (Salesforce License) — includes the full CRM object set, none of which this application uses. It works, and it is the more expensive answer to a question asking for the optimal one.
Option D (Identity License) — provides single sign-on and the App Launcher so an employee can reach other applications. It does not grant the access to custom objects, Apex and Visualforce that using this platform requires.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A consumer products company uses Salesforce to maintain consumer information, including orders. The company implemented a portal solution using Salesforce Experience Cloud for its consumers where the consumers can log in using their credentials. The company is considering allowing users to login with their Facebook or LinkedIn credentials. Once enabled, what role will Salesforce play?
optionA: Salesforce will be the identity provider (IdP).
optionB: Salesforce will be the service provider (SP).
optionC: Facebook and LinkedIn will act as the IdPs and SPs.
optionD: Facebook and LinkedIn will be the SPs.
explanation:
Salesforce will be the service provider. The consumer is trying to reach the Experience Cloud portal, so Salesforce is the protected resource; Facebook and LinkedIn authenticate the person and assert that identity to Salesforce, which consumes it. Adding social login does not change what Salesforce is protecting, only who vouches for the user arriving.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce will be the identity provider) — reverses the roles. Salesforce would be the IdP if it were asserting its users' identities to some other application, which is not what enabling social login does.
Option C (Facebook and LinkedIn act as both IdPs and SPs) — half right and half invented. They are identity providers here; nothing in this scenario has anyone signing in to Facebook or LinkedIn using a Salesforce identity.
Option D (Facebook and LinkedIn will be the SPs) — the exact inversion. They are supplying the authentication, not consuming it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has implemented a multi-org strategy and would like to centralize the management of their Salesforce user profiles. What should the architect recommend to allow Salesforce profiles to be managed from a central system of record?
optionA: Implement an OAuth JWT flow to pass the profile credentials between systems.
optionB: Implement JIT provisioning on the SAML IdP that will pass the profile ID in each assertion.
optionC: Create an Apex scheduled job in one org that will synchronize the other orgs' profiles.
optionD: Implement Delegated Authentication that will update the user profiles as necessary.
explanation:
Just-in-Time provisioning on the SAML identity provider, passing the profile ID in every assertion, is the recommendation. The IdP becomes the single system of record: each login carries the profile the user should have, and the JIT handler in each org reads that attribute and sets the User's profile accordingly — so a change made centrally lands in every org the next time the user signs in there.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an OAuth JWT flow passing profile credentials between systems) — the JWT bearer flow authorizes a client application to act for a known user. It is an authentication mechanism and carries no profile assignment.
Option C (an Apex scheduled job in one org synchronising the others' profiles) — profiles are metadata rather than records, an org cannot reach into another org's user configuration this way, and the arrangement makes one Salesforce org the master rather than the central system of record the question specifies.
Option D (Delegated Authentication updating profiles as necessary) — has Salesforce call an external service to verify a password. It returns a yes or no on the credential and updates nothing about the user.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is creating a mobile application that will be secured by Salesforce Identity using the OAuth 2.0 User-Agent flow (this flow uses the OAuth 2.0 implicit grant type). Which three OAuth concepts apply to this flow? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Verification Code
optionB: Authorization Code
optionC: Scopes
optionD: Client ID
explanation:
The User-Agent, or implicit grant, flow uses three of the concepts listed: Client ID identifies the connected app in the initial redirect, Scopes declare what the issued token may access, and a Refresh Token can come back alongside the access token.
The refresh token deserves care, because the strict OAuth 2.0 specification does not allow one in the implicit grant and Salesforce's implementation extends it. Requesting the scope is necessary but not sufficient: Salesforce documents that 'the refresh token for the user-agent flow is only issued if you requested scope=refresh_token' AND the redirect URL meets one of a small set of conditions — a custom protocol, a matching host using the oauth2/success servlet, or one of the mobileauth.salesforce.com URLs. So E is right for this flow as Salesforce implements it, but a plain https redirect URL with the scope requested still gets no refresh token.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Verification Code) — belongs to the Device Authentication Flow, where a device with no browser displays a code for the user to enter on another machine.
Option B (Authorization Code) — is precisely what separates the Web Server flow from this one. The implicit grant returns the access token directly in the redirect URL fragment, with no code to exchange server-to-server.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.remoteaccess_oauth_user_agent_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants Salesforce inbound OAuth-enabled integration clients to use SAML-based single sign-on for authentication. What OAuth flow would be recommended in this scenario?
optionA: SAML Assertion OAuth Flow
optionB: User-Token OAuth Flow
optionC: User-Agent OAuth Flow
optionD: Web Server OAuth Flow
explanation:
The SAML Assertion OAuth Flow is the recommendation. It lets an integration client that has already authenticated the user through the corporate SAML identity provider present that assertion to Salesforce and receive an OAuth access token in return — turning the existing single sign-on into API access without asking anyone to log in a second time.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (User-Token OAuth Flow) — not a Salesforce OAuth flow. The name is invented.
Option C (User-Agent OAuth Flow) — redirects a browser so the user can approve access interactively, and returns the token in a URL fragment. It is a flow for client-side applications with a user present, and it makes no use of the SAML configuration the requirement is built on.
Option D (Web Server OAuth Flow) — also depends on a browser redirect and an authorization code exchange, so it authenticates the user afresh at Salesforce rather than accepting the SAML assertion the client already holds.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_SAML_bearer_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_web_sso_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is planning to deploy a custom mobile app that will allow users to get e-signatures from its customers on their mobile devices. The mobile app connects to Salesforce to upload the e-signature as a file attachment and uses OAuth protocol for both authentication and authorization. What is the most recommended and secure OAuth scope setting that an architect should recommend?
optionA: api
optionB: id
optionC: custom_permissions
optionD: web
explanation:
The api scope is the most secure setting that still meets the requirement. Uploading an e-signature as a file attachment is an API write, so api is the narrowest scope that does the job — least privilege applied to the connected app.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (id) — returns the identity URL so the app can learn who the user is. It grants no access to records, so no attachment could be uploaded with it.
Option C (custom_permissions) — exposes which custom permissions the user holds, as information. It is not an access grant at all.
Option D (web) — allows the token to open a Salesforce user-interface session through frontdoor.jsp. That is broader than this app needs and unrelated to an API upload.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which two are valid choices for digital certificates when setting up two-way SSL between Salesforce and an external system? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use a trusted CA-signed certificate for Salesforce and a trusted CA-signed cert for the external system.
optionB: Use a self-signed certificate for Salesforce and a trusted CA-signed cert for the external system.
optionC: Use a trusted CA-signed certificate for Salesforce and a self-signed cert for the external system.
optionD: Use a self-signed certificate for Salesforce and a self-signed cert for the external system.
explanation:
Two-way SSL requires each side to validate what the other presents, so the workable combinations are the ones where that validation can succeed in both directions.
Both sides CA-signed is the straightforward posture: trust derives from a root authority each side already holds, and Salesforce publishes the roots it accepts at /cacerts.jsp. Salesforce also documents that a client certificate obtained from a Public CA 'must chain to a valid Root CA for your instance' and, for mutual authentication, 'must include the Client Authentication EKU'.
Both sides self-signed can also be made to work, but only because trust is established by explicit exchange rather than by a CA: for inbound mutual authentication 'Salesforce checks the certificate and chain against the certificate that you upload in your Certificate and Key Management settings', and a certificate Salesforce presents outbound has to be installed in the target server's keystore. Every renewal then has to be re-exchanged on both sides, which is why this option suits controlled or non-production integrations rather than public ones.
Be aware of two current constraints that bear on the CA-signed choice: certificates must include all intermediates in the chain, and under Chrome Root Program Policy v1.7 your client and server certificates 'can't originate from the same Public Root CA', so a single hierarchy for both roles is no longer viable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (self-signed for Salesforce, CA-signed for the external system) — a mismatched pair. This item treats the certificate choice as one decision applied to both ends, and the mix takes on the per-certificate exchange and rotation burden of the self-signed side while still paying for issuance on the other.
Option C (CA-signed for Salesforce, self-signed for the external system) — the same mismatch reversed, with the manual trust step landing on Salesforce instead. Neither mixed pairing is impossible to configure; both simply combine the costs of the two clean options without the benefit of either.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_keys_uploading_mutual_auth_cert.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000383575&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Key A,D left in place, but flagged as a judgement call rather than confirmed, because the documentation does not settle it as cleanly as the deck implies. What is documented: for inbound mTLS Salesforce validates the client chain against a certificate you upload, which is what makes a self-signed pairing workable, and Salesforce can present a self-signed certificate outbound if the target installs it. What is not documented anywhere I could render: any statement that the asymmetric combinations B and C are invalid. They are coherent configurations, so the item's premise that only the symmetric pairs are 'valid choices' rests on a symmetry intuition rather than a source. I did not reletter the key, since A and D are genuinely workable and no documentation contradicts them; the honest repair would be to reword the stem toward 'most commonly used' rather than 'valid'. The explanation now states the real constraints, including the Chrome Root Program v1.7 rule against sharing one root CA for client and server certificates.

question: Universal Containers (UC) has an existing Salesforce org configured for SP-initiated SAML SSO with their IdP. A second Salesforce org is being introduced into the environment and the IT team would like to ensure they can use the same IdP for the new org. What action should the IT team take while implementing the second org?
optionA: Use the same request bindings as the first org.
optionB: Use the same SAML Identity Location as the first org.
optionC: Use the Salesforce Username as the SAML Identity Type.
optionD: Use a different Entity ID than the first org.
explanation:
The second org must use a different Entity ID from the first. The Entity ID is how a service provider identifies itself to the identity provider, and the IdP uses it to select which service provider configuration — certificate, assertion consumer service URL, attribute mapping — to apply. Two Salesforce orgs presenting the same Entity ID would collide there, so the new org needs its own value and its own registration at the IdP.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (use the same request bindings as the first org) — bindings describe how the message travels, such as HTTP POST or Redirect. Matching them changes nothing about telling the two orgs apart.
Option B (use the same SAML Identity Location as the first org) — says where in the assertion the user's identifier sits, in the Subject or an attribute. It identifies the user, not the org.
Option C (use the Salesforce Username as the SAML Identity Type) — a choice about which field the assertion's identifier maps to. Either setting can be right, and neither distinguishes one service provider from another.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_saml_sso.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A global fitness equipment manufacturer is planning to sell fitness tracking devices and has the following requirements: (1) Customer purchases the device; (2) Customer registers the device using their mobile app; (3) A case should automatically be created in Salesforce and associated with the customer's account in cases where the device registers issues with tracking. Which OAuth flow should be used to meet these requirements?
optionA: OAuth 2.0 Username-Password Flow
optionB: OAuth 2.0 Asset Token Flow
optionC: OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow
optionD: OAuth 2.0 User-Agent Flow
explanation:
The OAuth 2.0 Asset Token Flow is the one to use. It ties each tracking device to an Asset record in Salesforce and issues a token scoped to that device, so when the device reports a tracking issue the case it creates is already associated with the right asset and therefore the right customer account — which is the third requirement.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Username-Password Flow) — puts a username and password on every device shipped, with no per-device identity to revoke and no link to an asset. It is also the flow Salesforce is retiring for connected apps.
Option C (SAML Bearer Assertion Flow) — exchanges an existing SAML assertion for a token on behalf of a user an identity provider has already authenticated. A fitness tracker has no SAML identity.
Option D (User-Agent Flow) — needs a browser to redirect and a person to approve access. The device registers once through the mobile app and thereafter reports on its own, with nobody watching.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_asset_token_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A company's external application is protected by Salesforce through OAuth. The identity architect for the project needs to limit the level of access to the data of the protected resource in a flexible way. What should be done to improve security?
optionA: Select 'Admin approved users are pre-authorized' and assign specific profiles.
optionB: Define a permission set that grants access to the app and assign to authorized users.
optionC: Leverage external objects and data classification policies.
optionD: Create custom scopes and assign to the Connected App.
explanation:
Custom scopes assigned to the Connected App are what add flexibility here. A custom scope lets the protected resource define permissions of its own — read against write, or one data set against another — which are then requested at token issuance and checked by the resource server on each call. That is finer-grained than deciding only whether an application may connect at all.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A ('Admin approved users are pre-authorized' with specific profiles) — controls which people may use the connected app. It is a yes-or-no gate on access, and it says nothing about how much of the protected resource's data a token may reach.
Option B (a permission set granting access to the app) — the same limitation in a different container: it decides who gets in, not what their token is allowed to do once there.
Option C (external objects and data classification policies) — external objects surface outside data inside Salesforce, and data classification is metadata describing sensitivity. Neither one constrains what an OAuth token can retrieve from the protected resource.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_customscopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to secure its Salesforce APIs by using an existing Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) configuration that supports the company's single sign-on process to Salesforce. Which Salesforce OAuth authorization flow should be used?
optionA: OAuth 2.0 User-Agent Flow
optionB: OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer Flow
optionC: OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow
optionD: SAML Assertion Flow
explanation:
Salesforce documents two different ways to turn SAML into API access, and this item turns on choosing between them.
The OAuth 2.0 SAML bearer assertion flow is the mainstream OAuth authorization flow for the job: 'a client—via a connected app—can use previous authorization by supplying a signed SAML 2.0 assertion to request an OAuth access token. The digital signature applied to the SAML assertion authenticates the authorized app.' The assertion is posted to the token endpoint, which 'issues an access_token based on prior approval of the app', so the existing SAML trust is reused while the connected app gives administrators a place to approve and govern each client. Since the question asks which OAuth authorization flow should be used, this is the answer.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (OAuth 2.0 User-Agent Flow) — redirects a browser and asks the user to approve access, returning the token in a URL fragment. It uses none of the existing SAML configuration and suits an interactive client rather than an API integration.
Option B (OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer Flow) — the same shape as the answer but built on a signed JSON Web Token. It is the right choice when trust is expressed as a JWT; here the company already has SAML.
Option D (SAML Assertion Flow) — real, and worth knowing rather than dismissing. It 'is an alternative for orgs that use SAML to access Salesforce and want to access the API the same way', and it 'can be used without a connected app'. Salesforce frames it as an alternative rather than an OAuth authorization flow, and it carries limits the bearer flow does not: it cannot be used with more than one org, and authentication through it does not invoke login flows. The discriminator is governance — choose the bearer assertion flow when clients should be registered and approved as connected apps, which is the normal posture for securing APIs.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_SAML_bearer_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_web_sso_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key C left in place, but flagged: this is the one item in the deck where I could not settle the answer decisively, and the user should decide. The case for C is that the question asks which OAuth authorization flow 'should be used', and the SAML bearer assertion flow is the mainstream one for API access via SAML, running through a connected app; Salesforce explicitly calls the plain SAML assertion flow 'an alternative' and documents real limitations on it. The case for D is the stem's wording, which paraphrases the assertion flow's opening sentence almost exactly — 'an existing SAML configuration that supports the company's single sign-on process to Salesforce' against 'orgs that use SAML to access Salesforce and want to access the API the same way'. Unlike the deck's other SAML-flow question, this stem contains no requirement that administrators authorise consuming apps, which is the requirement that cleanly selects bearer elsewhere in the deck. Review this together with the question keyed to the SAML Assertion Flow: the two stems are close enough that whichever way this one is decided, both should be worded so the discriminator is visible.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters wants to implement a partner community. Active community users will need to review and accept the community rules, and update key contact information for each community member before their annual partner event. Which approach will meet this requirement?
optionA: Create a login flow that conditionally prompts users who have not accepted the new community rules and who have missing or outdated information.
optionB: Add a banner to the Community Home page asking users to update their profile and accept the new community rules.
optionC: Create a custom landing page and email campaign asking all community members to login and verify their data.
optionD: Create tasks for users who need to update their data or accept the new community rules.
explanation:
A login flow that conditionally prompts the affected users is the approach that meets this. A login flow runs between successful authentication and access to the community, so it can show the rules for acceptance and a data-update screen to exactly those members who have not yet accepted or whose contact details are stale — and withhold access until they do. Enforcement before entry is what the requirement needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a banner on the Community Home page) — asks rather than requires. Members can ignore it indefinitely, and it appears to everyone including those who have already complied.
Option C (a custom landing page and email campaign) — depends on people reading an email and acting on it, so there is no guarantee the rules are accepted before the event.
Option D (tasks for the users who need to act) — records the intent internally, and community members are not working a Salesforce task list. Nothing about it blocks access to the community.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_login_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A third-party app provider would like to have users provisioned via a service endpoint before users access their app from Salesforce. What should an identity architect recommend to configure the requirement with limited changes to the third-party app?
optionA: Redirect users to the third-party app for registration.
optionB: Use Salesforce Identity with SAML for provisioning users.
optionC: Create a Canvas app in Salesforce for the third-party app to provision users.
optionD: Use a Connected App with user provisioning flow.
explanation:
A Connected App with the user provisioning flow is the recommendation. Salesforce's User Provisioning pushes lifecycle events to the third-party application's service endpoint declaratively, so users are created there before they arrive from Salesforce — and the third-party side only has to expose the provisioning endpoint it already has, which is the 'limited changes' the question asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (redirect users to the third-party app for registration) — provisions on arrival rather than before it, and pushes work onto the user and onto the third-party application's registration screens.
Option B (Salesforce Identity with SAML for provisioning) — SAML authenticates users; it does not call a provisioning endpoint. Just-in-Time provisioning built on it would also act at first login, after the point the requirement specifies.
