Option C (a Canvas app for the third-party app to provision users) — Canvas embeds an external application inside Salesforce. It is a presentation mechanism, and it would require substantial work on the third-party side, which the requirement rules out.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_user_provisioning.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is using OpenID Connect to enable a connection from their new mobile app to its production Salesforce org. What should be done to enable the retrieval of the access token status for the OpenID Connect connection?
optionA: Leverage OpenID Connect Token Introspection.
optionB: Create a custom OAuth scope.
optionC: Query using OpenID Connect Discovery endpoint.
optionD: Enable Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) for the /services/oauth2/token endpoint.
explanation:
OpenID Connect Token Introspection is what retrieves an access token's status. Salesforce exposes the introspection endpoint from the standard, which lets a client or resource server ask the issuer whether a given token is still active and what claims it carries — the question being asked here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (create a custom OAuth scope) — defines a new permission that a token can carry. It shapes what a token may do, not how you find out whether it is still valid.
Option C (query the OpenID Connect Discovery endpoint) — returns the configuration of the provider itself: endpoint URLs, supported scopes, signing keys. It describes the service, and knows nothing about any individual token.
Option D (enable CORS for the /services/oauth2/token endpoint) — allows a browser on another origin to call that endpoint. It is a cross-origin permission, unrelated to reporting a token's state.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oidc_token_introspection_endpoint.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is planning to roll out a partner portal for its distributors using Experience Cloud. NTO would like to use an external identity provider (IdP) and for partners to register for access to the portal. Each partner should be allowed to register only once to avoid duplicate accounts with Salesforce. What should an identity architect recommend to create partners?
optionA: Create a custom page in Experience Cloud to self-register partners with Experience Cloud and the Ping identity store.
optionB: Allow partners to register through the IdP and create partner users in Salesforce through an API.
optionC: Create a custom web page in the portal and create users in the IdP and Experience Cloud using published APIs.
optionD: On successful creation of partners using the Self Registration page in Experience Cloud, create the identity in Ping.
explanation:
Letting partners register through the identity provider, with partner users then created in Salesforce through an API, is the recommendation. It makes the IdP the single place a partner registers, which is what stops a second registration producing a duplicate account, and Salesforce is populated as a consequence of that one event rather than through a competing path.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom Experience Cloud page registering partners in both Experience Cloud and the Ping identity store) — writes to two systems from one page, so a partial failure leaves the two out of step, and it keeps a second registration surface open.
Option C (a custom web page in the portal creating users in the IdP and Experience Cloud via APIs) — the same dual-write problem with the page moved. Two systems are still being created in parallel rather than one following the other.
Option D (create the identity in Ping after a successful Experience Cloud self-registration) — inverts the source of truth. Registration begins in Salesforce, so nothing stops the same partner registering again through the IdP, which is the duplicate the requirement forbids.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_scim_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has implemented SAML SSO to enable seamless access across multiple applications. UC has regional Salesforce orgs and wants its users to be able to access them from their main Salesforce org seamlessly. Which action should an architect recommend?
optionA: Configure the main Salesforce org as a Service Provider.
optionB: Configure the main Salesforce org as an Authentication Provider.
optionC: Configure the main Salesforce org as the Identity Provider.
optionD: Configure the regional Salesforce orgs as Identity Providers.
explanation:
The main Salesforce org should be configured as the Identity Provider. Salesforce can issue SAML assertions as well as consume them, so the main org authenticates the user once and asserts that identity to each regional org, which becomes a service provider — and the App Launcher gives users the tiles to move between them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (configure the main org as a Service Provider) — is its role in the existing arrangement with the corporate IdP. It does nothing to get users from the main org into the regional ones, which needs the main org to assert identity outward.
Option B (configure the main org as an Authentication Provider) — an Auth Provider is configuration for accepting logins from an external OpenID Connect or OAuth service. It points inward, and it is not a role one org holds for another.
Option D (configure the regional orgs as Identity Providers) — reverses the direction of travel. Users start in the main org, so making each regional org an IdP would ask them to authenticate at the destination they are trying to reach.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_sfdc_both_sp_idp.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identity_provider_enable.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a custom, internal-only mobile billing application for users who are commonly out of the office. The app is configured as a Connected App in Salesforce. Due to the nature of this app, UC would like to take the appropriate measures to properly secure access to the app. Which two are recommendations to make to UC? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Require High Assurance sessions in order to use the Connected App.
optionB: Use Google Authenticator (or Salesforce Authenticator) as an additional part of the login process.
optionC: Set Login IP Ranges to the internal network for all of the app users' profiles.
optionD: Disallow the use of Single Sign-On for any users of the mobile app.
explanation:
Two measures fit an internal application used from outside the office. Requiring High Assurance sessions on the Connected App means the app cannot be opened until the user's session has been raised by identity verification. Adding an authenticator app as a second factor is what raises it, and it defends the account against a stolen password wherever the user happens to be.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (set Login IP Ranges to the internal network on all the app users' profiles) — contradicts the scenario. These users are commonly out of the office, so restricting logins to internal addresses would lock them out of the app they need.
Option D (disallow Single Sign-On for mobile app users) — weakens security rather than strengthening it, by removing users from centrally managed authentication policy and pushing them back onto org-local passwords.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_require_two_factor_authentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.connected_app_manage_session_policies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_overview_2fa.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A global fitness equipment manufacturer uses Salesforce to manage its sales cycle. The manufacturer has a custom order fulfillment app that needs to request order data from Salesforce. The order fulfillment app needs to integrate with the Salesforce API using the OAuth 2.0 protocol. What should an identity architect use to fulfill this requirement?
optionA: Authentication Providers
optionB: Canvas App Integration
optionC: OAuth Tokens
optionD: Connected App and OAuth scopes
explanation:
A Connected App with OAuth scopes is what this requires. Any external application calling the Salesforce API over OAuth has to be registered as a connected app — that is where the consumer key, callback URL and permitted users live — and the scopes on it define what the tokens it receives may do, such as api for REST access to order data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Authentication Providers) — configure Salesforce to accept logins from an external service such as Google or an OpenID Connect provider. That is inbound identity, not an application calling the Salesforce API.
Option B (Canvas App Integration) — embeds an external application's user interface inside Salesforce pages. The fulfilment app needs data, not a place to render.
Option C (OAuth Tokens) — the credentials the flow produces. They are the result of registering a connected app, not the thing an architect configures to enable the integration.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_scopes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to implement Delegated Authentication for a certain subset of Salesforce users. Which three items should UC take into consideration while building the web service to handle the Delegated Authentication request? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: UC should whitelist all Salesforce IP ranges on their corporate firewall.
optionB: The web service needs to include sourceIp as a method parameter.
optionC: The web service can be written using either the SOAP or REST protocol.
optionD: Delegated Authentication is enabled for the System Administrator profile.
optionE: The return type of the web service method should be a Boolean value.
explanation:
Three items matter when building a Delegated Authentication web service.
Whitelist Salesforce IP ranges on the corporate firewall — Salesforce makes an outbound SOAP call to the delegated authentication endpoint on every login, so the firewall must permit traffic from Salesforce's published egress ranges.
Include sourceIp as a method parameter — the WSDL Salesforce publishes defines exactly three inputs: username, password and sourceIp. The service can use sourceIp for IP-based decisions of its own.
Return a Boolean — the method must answer true for valid credentials or false for invalid, and Salesforce uses that value directly to approve or reject the login.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (the service can be written using either SOAP or REST) — Delegated Authentication is SOAP only. The published WSDL defines the whole contract, and a REST endpoint cannot fulfil it.
Option D (Delegated Authentication is enabled for the System Administrator profile) — a dangerous distractor rather than a consideration. If the endpoint goes down and administrators depend on it, nobody can log in to diagnose the outage; keep at least one System Administrator on standard Salesforce authentication as a recovery path.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication_tips.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is building a custom employee hub application on Amazon Web Services (AWS) and would like to store their users' credentials there. Users will also need access to Salesforce for internal operations. UC has tasked an identity architect with evaluating different solutions for authentication and authorization between AWS and Salesforce. How should an identity architect configure AWS to authenticate and authorize Salesforce users?
optionA: Create a custom external authentication provider.
optionB: Configure the custom employee app as a Connected App.
optionC: Configure AWS as an OpenID Connect Provider.
optionD: Develop a custom Auth server in AWS.
explanation:
Configuring AWS as an OpenID Connect Provider is the answer. Salesforce accepts OpenID Connect natively through an authentication provider, so an AWS-hosted OIDC service issuing tokens for the employee hub's credential store becomes a trusted login source for Salesforce — a standard protocol on both sides, with no bespoke code in between.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (create a custom external authentication provider) — the fallback for a service that speaks neither OpenID Connect nor one of the predefined provider types. Choosing it here means writing and maintaining a custom authentication provider class for a protocol Salesforce already supports out of the box.
Option B (configure the custom employee app as a Connected App) — points the wrong way. A connected app lets Salesforce assert identity outward to an application; the requirement is for Salesforce to accept identities that AWS asserts.
Option D (develop a custom Auth server in AWS) — builds an identity provider from scratch when AWS already offers one. It is the most work and the largest security surface for the same outcome.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_authentication_providers.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has an existing e-commerce platform and is implementing a new customer community. They do not want to force customers to register on both applications due to concern over the customer experience. It is expected that 25% of the e-commerce customers will utilize the customer community. The e-commerce platform is capable of generating SAML responses and has an existing RESTful API capable of managing users. How should UC create the identities of its e-commerce users with the customer community?
optionA: Use the standard Salesforce API to create users in the community when a user is created in the e-commerce platform and use SAML to allow SSO.
optionB: Use SAML JIT in the customer community to create users when a user tries to login to the community from the e-commerce site.
optionC: Use the e-commerce REST API to create users when a user self-registers on the customer community and use SAML to allow SSO.
optionD: Use a nightly batch ETL job to sync users between the customer community and the e-commerce platform and use SAML to allow SSO.
explanation:
SAML Just-in-Time provisioning in the customer community is how these identities should be created. The e-commerce platform can already produce SAML responses, so a customer who follows a link into the community arrives with an assertion, and JIT creates their community user at that moment from the attributes it carries. Nobody registers twice, and users exist only once they actually turn up.
That last point is what the numbers in the stem are for: only a quarter of the e-commerce base is expected to use the community, so provisioning on demand avoids creating three users for every one that logs in.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (create community users through the Salesforce API whenever one is created on the e-commerce platform) — provisions everybody in advance, including the 75% who never arrive, and adds an integration to build and keep running.
Option C (call the e-commerce REST API when a user self-registers on the community) — reverses the direction. It opens a second registration surface, which is exactly the double registration the customer experience concern rules out.
Option D (a nightly batch ETL sync) — provisions everybody like option A, and adds up to a day's delay, so a customer who registers on the e-commerce site in the morning cannot enter the community until the next day.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is using Salesforce Experience Cloud site for its container wholesale business. The identity architect wants to create an authentication provider for the new site. Which two options should be utilized in creating an authentication provider? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: A custom registration handler can be set.
optionB: The default authentication provider certificate can be set.
optionC: A custom error URL can be set.
optionD: The default login user can be set.
explanation:
Two of these are genuine authentication provider settings. A custom registration handler can be set — the Apex class or flow that decides how the attributes returned by the provider create or update a Salesforce user. A custom error URL can be set too, so that a failed authentication lands the user on a page of UC's choosing rather than a generic error.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the default authentication provider certificate can be set) — there is no such field. Certificates come into SAML single sign-on configuration; an auth provider is configured with a consumer key and secret from the external service.
Option D (the default login user can be set) — not an auth provider setting either. Which user a login resolves to is determined by the registration handler, from the identity the provider returns.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_provider_linkedin.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_create_registration_handler.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers built a custom mobile app for their field reps to create orders in Salesforce. OAuth is used for authenticating mobile users. The app is built in such a way that when a user session expires after initial login, a new access token is obtained automatically without forcing the user to log in again. While that improved the field reps' productivity, UC realized that they need a 'logout' feature. What should the logout function perform in this scenario, where user sessions are refreshed automatically?
optionA: Clear out the Client ID to stop auto session refresh.
optionB: Clear out all the tokens to stop auto session refresh.
optionC: Invoke the revocation URL and pass the access token.
optionD: Invoke the revocation URL and pass the refresh token.
explanation:
Logout must invoke the revocation URL and pass the refresh token. The refresh token is what keeps the session alive, so revoking it at the endpoint invalidates it server-side and breaks the automatic renewal chain. Nothing short of that is a logout in an app built this way.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (clear out the Client ID) — the client ID identifies the application, not the session, and it is the same value for every user. Removing it would break the app rather than log anyone out.
Option B (clear out all the tokens locally) — removes the credentials from this device but leaves them valid on the server, so an intercepted or backed-up refresh token still works. Local cleanup is worth doing alongside revocation, not instead of it.
Option C (invoke the revocation URL with the access token) — the near miss, and it revokes the shorter-lived half. The refresh token survives and mints a new access token immediately, so the user is never actually logged out.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_revoke_token.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to implement Single Sign-On for a Salesforce org using an external Identity Provider and corporate identity store. What type of authentication flow is required to support deep linking?
optionA: Service-Provider-Initiated SSO
optionB: Identity-Provider-Initiated SSO
optionC: Web Server OAuth SSO flow
optionD: Start URL on Identity Provider
explanation:
Service-Provider-Initiated SSO is what supports deep linking. The user starts at the Salesforce resource they want, so Salesforce builds the SAML AuthnRequest and puts the requested destination in RelayState. The identity provider hands that value back untouched, and Salesforce sends the user to the record they originally asked for rather than a default page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Identity-Provider-Initiated SSO) — starts at the IdP, which posts an assertion to Salesforce with no knowledge of any particular record. The user lands on the default destination.
Option C (Web Server OAuth SSO flow) — authorizes an application to call APIs on a user's behalf. It is not the SAML single sign-on the question describes, and it carries no RelayState.
Option D (a Start URL on the identity provider) — sets one fixed landing page for everyone. That is the opposite of deep linking, which needs a different destination per request.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000315559&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000386068&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers (UC) is looking to build a Canvas app and wants to use the corresponding Connected App to control where the app is visible. Which two options are correct in regards to where the app can be made visible under the Connected App setting for the Canvas app? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The sidebar of a Salesforce Console as a console component.
optionB: Included in the Call Control Tool that's part of Open CTI.
optionC: As part of the body of a Salesforce Knowledge article.
optionD: In the mobile navigation menu on Salesforce for Android.
explanation:
Where a canvas app can appear is governed by the Locations field of the Canvas app settings on its connected app, and the documented values are Chatter Feed, Chatter Tab, Console, Layouts and Mobile Cards, Lightning Component, Mobile Nav, Open CTI, Publisher, and Visualforce Page.
Two of those match the keyed answers directly. 'Console—The canvas app appears in the footer or sidebars of a Salesforce console. If this option is selected, you must choose where the canvas app appears in a console by adding it as a custom console component.' And 'Mobile Nav—The canvas app is accessible from the mobile app navigation menu.'
Be aware that this item is defective as a choose-two. Open CTI is also a documented Locations value, so three of the four options are correct and only one is genuinely false.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (included in the Call Control Tool that is part of Open CTI) — this one is not actually wrong. Salesforce documents it: 'Open CTI—The canvas app appears in the call control tool. If this option is selected, you must specify the canvas app in your call center's definition file for it to appear.' It is the reason the item cannot be answered cleanly, and it is left unkeyed here only because the item asks for two.
Option C (as part of the body of a Salesforce Knowledge article) — the only genuinely false option. Nothing in the Canvas documentation places a canvas app inside a Knowledge article body, and it is the one choice that appears nowhere in the Locations list.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_connect.meta/platform_connect/canvas_apps_where_they_appear.htm

corrected.note: Key A,D left in place because both are correct, but the item is defective and the explanation now says so. Option B is equally correct: Open CTI is one of the nine documented values of the Locations field, described as making the canvas app appear in the call control tool, and the same page separately lists 'In an Open CTI call control tool after you add it to the call center's definition file' among the places canvas apps appear. So this is a choose-two with three true options. Only option C is false — Knowledge is not mentioned anywhere on the page. Flagged for the user: the clean repair is either to convert this to a choose-three, or to replace option B with a second genuinely false location, since as printed a well-prepared candidate can pick A, B or D and be right.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) uses the Customer 360 Platform implemented on Salesforce Experience Cloud. The development team in charge has learned of a contactless user feature, which can reduce the overhead of managing customers and partners by creating users without contact information. What is the potential impact to the architecture if NTO decides to implement this feature?
optionA: Custom registration handler is needed to correctly assign External Identity or Community license for the newly registered contactless user.
optionB: Passwordless authentication cannot be supported because the mobile phone receiving the one-time password (OTP) needs to match the number on the contact record.
optionC: If a contactless user is upgraded to a Community license, the contact record is automatically created and linked to the user record, but not associated with an Account.
optionD: Contactless user feature is available only with the External Identity license, which can restrict the Experience Cloud functionality available to the user.
explanation:
The contactless user feature is available only with the External Identity license, and that licensing constraint is the architectural impact. Adopting it to avoid managing contact records also accepts the narrower Experience Cloud functionality an External Identity user has, compared with a Community licence holder who works with records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom registration handler is needed to assign the right license) — invents a requirement. The license follows from how the user is created and the profile assigned; no handler is needed to pick between External Identity and Community for a contactless user.
Option B (passwordless authentication cannot be supported because the phone must match the contact record) — states the opposite of the point of the feature. A contactless user has no contact record, and the verification method is registered against the user, which is what makes passwordless login work for them.
Option C (upgrading to a Community license creates a contact automatically but leaves it unassociated with an Account) — half describes the upgrade path and then adds a defect that is not documented. A contact created this way is not left floating without an account.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_manage_create_contactless_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_licenses.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which three different attributes can be used to identify the user in a SAML assertion when Salesforce is acting as a Service Provider? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: User Full Name
optionB: Salesforce Username
optionC: User Email Address
optionD: Salesforce User ID
explanation:
Salesforce can match the user in an incoming assertion by one of three identifiers, which is what the SAML Identity Type setting selects: the Salesforce Username, the Salesforce User ID, or the Federation ID stored on the user record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (User Full Name) — not an identity type, and not unique. Two users can share a name, so it could never resolve an assertion to one record.
Option C (User Email Address) — likewise not one of the identity types Salesforce offers here. Email is commonly what an identity provider sends, but it has to arrive in the assertion as the username or as the Federation ID value to be matched.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_service_provider_configuration.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers allows employees to use a mobile device to access Salesforce for daily operations using a hybrid mobile app. This app uses Mobile SDKs, leverages refresh tokens to regenerate access tokens when required, and is distributed as a private app. The chief security officer is rolling out an org-wide compliance policy to enforce re-verification of devices if an employee has not logged in from that device in the last week. Which Connected App setting should be leveraged to comply with this policy change?
optionA: Scope - Deny refresh_token scope for this Connected App.
optionB: Permitted Users - Ask admins to maintain a list of users who are permitted based on last login date.
optionC: Session Policy - Set timeout value of the Connected App to 7 days.
optionD: Refresh Token Policy - Expire the refresh token if it has not been used for 7 days.
explanation:
The Refresh Token Policy is the setting to use, set to expire the refresh token if it has not been used for 7 days. That maps directly onto the compliance requirement: a device idle for a week loses its refresh token, so the next attempt cannot renew silently and the employee has to authenticate and re-verify the device.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (deny the refresh_token scope for the Connected App) — over-corrects. Without refresh tokens the app prompts for credentials constantly, discarding the productivity the design was built for rather than re-verifying after a week of disuse.
Option B (have admins maintain a list of permitted users by last login date) — turns an automatic policy into manual administration, and Permitted Users controls who may use the app at all, not how recently they used it.
Option C (set the Connected App session timeout to 7 days) — governs how long an established session lasts, not how long an unused refresh token survives. A session timing out is exactly the case the refresh token silently repairs, so this changes nothing about device re-verification.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.connected_app_manage_oauth.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Under which scenario will the Web Server flow be used?
optionA: Used for server-side components when a page needs to be rendered.
optionB: Used for mobile applications and testing legacy integrations.
optionC: Used for verifying access to protected resources.
optionD: Used for web applications when server-side code needs to interact with APIs.
explanation:
The Web Server flow is used by web applications whose server-side code needs to call APIs. The browser is redirected to Salesforce, the user authorizes, an authorization code comes back to the application's server, and the server exchanges that code — using a client secret it can keep private — for an access token and a refresh token to call the API with.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (server-side components when a page needs to be rendered) — describes rendering rather than API access, and every OAuth flow ends with a page being rendered. It names no property that distinguishes this flow.
Option B (mobile applications and testing legacy integrations) — points at other flows: the user-agent flow was the traditional mobile answer, and the username-password flow was the legacy testing shortcut.
Option C (verifying access to protected resources) — describes what an access token is for once any flow has issued one, not the scenario that selects this particular flow.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_web_server_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: In an SP-initiated SAML SSO setup where the user tries to access a resource on the Service Provider, what HTTP parameter should be used when submitting a SAML request to the IdP, to ensure the user is returned to the intended resource after authentication?
optionA: DisplayState
optionB: RedirectURL
optionC: RelayState
optionD: StartURL
explanation:
RelayState is the parameter to use. The service provider sets it on the SAML request, the identity provider treats it as opaque and returns it unchanged with the response, and the service provider then uses it to send the user to the resource they originally asked for instead of a default landing page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (DisplayState) — not a SAML parameter. The name does not appear in the specification or in Salesforce's SSO settings.
Option B (RedirectURL) — also not part of the SAML exchange. A redirect URL is OAuth vocabulary, where it names the callback a connected app is returned to.
Option D (StartURL) — a Salesforce parameter that sends a user to a page after login, but it is not what an SP-initiated SAML request carries to the identity provider for round-tripping.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000386068&language=en_US&type=1

question: An identity architect's client has a homegrown identity provider (IdP). Salesforce is used as the service provider (SP). The head of IT is worried that during an SP-initiated single sign-on (SSO), the SAML request content will be altered. What should the identity architect recommend to make sure that there is additional trust between the SP and the IdP?
optionA: Encrypt the SAML request using a CA-signed certificate and decrypt on the IdP.
optionB: Ensure that on the SSO settings page, the 'Request Signing Certificate' field has a self-signed certificate.
optionC: Ensure that the Issuer and Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL are properly configured between SP and IdP.
optionD: Ensure that there is an HTTPS connection between IdP and SP.
explanation:
Putting a certificate in the 'Request Signing Certificate' field on the SSO settings page is the recommendation. With that set, Salesforce signs the SAML AuthnRequest it sends, so any alteration of the request in flight invalidates the signature and the identity provider rejects it. That is the integrity guarantee the head of IT is asking for, and a self-signed certificate is sufficient because the identity provider is being given that specific certificate to trust.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (encrypt the SAML request with a CA-signed certificate and decrypt at the IdP) — solves confidentiality rather than integrity. Encryption hides the request's contents; it is signing that proves the contents did not change, which is the stated worry.
Option C (make sure the Issuer and Assertion Consumer Service URL are properly configured) — necessary for the exchange to function at all, and it establishes no trust. A correctly addressed request can still be tampered with in transit.
Option D (ensure an HTTPS connection between IdP and SP) — protects the channel between two endpoints. The SAML request travels through the user's browser, so a transport-level guarantee does not cover the party actually in a position to alter it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_service_provider_configuration.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is successfully using Delegated Authentication for their Salesforce users. The service supporting Delegated Authentication is written in Java. UC has a new CIO that is requiring all company web services be RESTful and written in .NET. Which two considerations should the UC architect provide to the new CIO? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Delegated Authentication will not work with REST services.
optionB: Delegated Authentication will continue to work with REST services.
optionC: Delegated Authentication will not work with a .NET service.
optionD: Delegated Authentication will continue to work with a .NET service.
explanation:
Two considerations belong in front of the CIO. Delegated Authentication will not work with REST services — the contract is SOAP, defined by a WSDL Salesforce publishes and calls, so there is no REST variant to build. But it will continue to work with a .NET service, because the implementation language is irrelevant as long as the SOAP contract is honoured. The blocker is the protocol, not the platform.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Delegated Authentication will continue to work with REST services) — contradicts the fixed SOAP contract. Salesforce calls the endpoint defined by its own WSDL, and a REST service cannot satisfy it.
Option C (Delegated Authentication will not work with a .NET service) — the wrong half of the CIO's mandate to object to. .NET serves SOAP perfectly well, and moving from Java to .NET costs nothing here.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication_tips.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: How should an architect automatically redirect users to the login page of the external Identity Provider when using an SP-initiated SAML flow with Salesforce as a Service Provider?
optionA: Enable the 'Redirect to the Identity Provider' setting under Authentication Services on the My Domain configuration.
optionB: Remove the Login Page from the list of Authentication Services on the My Domain configuration.
optionC: Set the Identity Provider as default and enable the 'Redirect to the Identity Provider' setting on the SAML configuration.
optionD: Use Visualforce as the landing page for My Domain to redirect users to the Identity Provider login page.
explanation:
Removing the Login Page from the list of Authentication Services in the My Domain configuration is what produces the automatic redirect. Authentication Services lists the ways users may authenticate at the My Domain URL; with the Salesforce login page taken out and the external identity provider left as the only service, a user arriving at that URL is sent straight to the provider's login page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (enable a 'Redirect to the Identity Provider' setting under Authentication Services) — names a setting that is not there. The behaviour is produced by which services are listed, not by a redirect checkbox.
Option C (set the identity provider as default and enable 'Redirect to the Identity Provider' on the SAML configuration) — invents the same non-existent switch, on the SAML page this time.
Option D (use a Visualforce page as the My Domain landing page to redirect users) — builds by hand what the configuration already does, and puts a page of custom code in the login path of every user.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.domain_name_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.domain_name_login_id_prov.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Customer service representatives at Universal Containers (UC) are complaining that whenever they click on links to case records and are asked to login with SAML SSO, they are being redirected to the Salesforce home tab and not the specific case record. What item should an architect advise the identity team at UC to investigate first?
optionA: The users have the correct Federation ID within Salesforce.
optionB: My Domain is configured and active within Salesforce.
optionC: The identity provider is correctly preserving the RelayState.
optionD: The Salesforce SSO settings are using HTTP POST.
explanation:
The first thing to investigate is whether the identity provider is correctly preserving the RelayState. The symptom is diagnostic: users reach Salesforce and are authenticated, but land on the home tab instead of the case they clicked. That is what happens when the deep-link context Salesforce put in RelayState is dropped or rewritten by the IdP, leaving Salesforce with no destination and falling back to the default.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (whether users have the correct Federation ID) — a wrong or missing Federation ID stops the login from succeeding at all. These users are being logged in, so identity matching is working.
Option B (whether My Domain is configured and active) — without My Domain the SP-initiated flow would not run in the first place, and no deep link would reach an IdP. It is already working here.
Option D (whether the SSO settings use HTTP POST) — the binding governs how the message is transmitted. A wrong binding produces a failed exchange, not a successful login that lands on the wrong page.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000386068&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000315559&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers' (UC) identity architect needs to recommend a license type for their new Experience Cloud site that will be used by external partners (delivery providers) for reviewing and updating their accounts, downloading files provided by UC, and obtaining scheduled pickup dates from their calendar. UC is using their Salesforce production org as the identity provider for these users and the expected number of individual users is 2.5 million with 13.5 million unique logins per month. Which of the following license types should be used to meet the requirement?
optionA: Partner Community Login License
optionB: Partner Community License
optionC: External Apps License
optionD: Customer Community Plus Login License
explanation:
The Partner Community Login License fits both halves of the requirement. Delivery providers acting on their own accounts are partners rather than end customers, which selects the Partner Community family; and the usage pattern — 2.5 million users generating 13.5 million logins a month, roughly five each — is what makes the login-based variant far cheaper than paying for every named member.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Partner Community License) — the right family, priced per member. With 2.5 million individuals logging in only a handful of times a month, paying for each named user is the expensive way to buy the same access.
Option C (External Apps License) — provides identity and light application access rather than the account collaboration these partners need for reviewing and updating their own accounts.
Option D (Customer Community Plus Login License) — the login-based pricing is right, and the family is wrong. These are partners, and Customer Community Plus is aimed at customers rather than at partner account access.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is using its production org as the identity provider for a new Experience Cloud site and the identity architect is deciding which login experience to use for the site. Which two page types are valid login page types for the site? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Embedded Login Page
optionB: Login Discovery Page
optionC: Lightning Experience Page
optionD: Experience Builder Page
explanation:
Salesforce documents a closed set of login page types, chosen on the Login & Registration page of the Administration workspace, and there are exactly four: Default Page, Login Discovery Page, Experience Builder Page, and Visualforce Page.
Two of them are the answers here. The Login Discovery Page is the type used 'to help you configure passwordless login. With passwordless login, you can let users log in with their email address or phone number.' The Experience Builder Page lets you 'quickly create and style a page that matches your company's brand' by dragging components in Experience Builder — with one restriction worth knowing: 'Unlike the other page types, the Experience Builder page limits users to logging in with a username and password', and the site must be published first.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Embedded Login Page) — not a login page type. Embedded Login is a separate Customer Identity feature that embeds login into an external website you host, and it sits alongside the login-page topics in the documentation rather than among the page-type options. It is also no longer a natural recommendation: Salesforce disabled it by default in Summer '24 because it relies on third-party cookies, and advises a redirect-based OAuth flow instead.
Option C (Lightning Experience Page) — no such login page type exists. The nearest real options are the Experience Builder Page for a declarative build and the Visualforce Page for a fully custom one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_login_discovery_login_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_login_pages_configure.htm&type=5&language=en_US

corrected.note: Answer moved A,B->B,D. The dedicated Login Page Types article carries a table of every valid type, and it contains Default Page, Login Discovery Page, Experience Builder Page and Visualforce Page — the word 'Embedded' does not appear in that table at all. The configuration article agrees, enumerating the same four values for the Login Page Type field. So option A named a real Salesforce feature that is not one of the answers to this question, and option D named an actual page type that the old key omitted. Embedded Login is separately documented as disabled by default since Summer '24 owing to third-party cookie restrictions, which makes keying it doubly wrong. Option C remains invented.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters wants to allow its consumers to self-register on its business-to-consumer (B2C) portal that is built on Experience Cloud. The identity architect has recommended using Person Accounts. Which three steps need to be configured to enable self-registration using Person Accounts? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Contact Salesforce Support to enable Person Accounts.
optionB: Enable access to Person and Business Account record types under Public Access Settings.
optionC: Under Login and Registration settings, ensure that the default Account field is empty.
optionD: Set organization-wide default sharing for Contact to Public Read Only.
optionE: Contact Salesforce Support to enable Business Accounts.
explanation:
Person accounts are the right model for a business-to-consumer portal, because when new users register 'they're added to your site under an individual record that merges account and contact information' — there is no separate business account to attach a contact to.
Three things have to be in place. Person Accounts must be turned on for the org. The site's guest and public access settings must permit the Person Account and Business Account record types, so a self-registering user can actually be created against them. And the Login & Registration configuration must not force everyone into one account: leaving the default Account field empty is what lets each registration create its own person account rather than being attached to a single shared one.
One currency correction to how the first step is often described. Enabling Person Accounts no longer requires a support request. Salesforce documents it as self-service: 'From Setup, enter Person Accounts in the Quick Find box, and then select Person Accounts. Go through the steps listed on the Setup page. Turn on Person Accounts', needing only the Customize Application and View All Profiles permissions. Read option A as 'enable Person Accounts', not as 'file a case'. Note also that the switch is one-way — 'After Person Accounts is enabled, it can't be disabled' — so preview it in a sandbox first.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option D (set organization-wide default sharing for Contact to Public Read Only) — a sharing decision about who can see contact records. It neither enables self-registration nor has any bearing on whether a person account can be created.
Option E (contact Salesforce Support to enable Business Accounts) — business accounts need no enablement at all. They are standard and available in every edition, so there is nothing to request.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.account_person_enable.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.external_identity_self_registration_person_accounts.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A,B,C left in place, but option A is stale and the explanation now says so. The Enable Person Accounts article describes a self-service Setup flow and never mentions Salesforce Support — the phrase does not appear on the page — and Salesforce shipped a release note specifically titled around enabling person accounts without contacting support. So A is correct in substance (Person Accounts must be enabled) and wrong in mechanism (a support request). I did not move the key because there is no fourth correct option to promote: D is wrong on sharing, and E is wrong because business accounts are standard in all editions and need no enablement. That makes this a choose-three with only two cleanly correct options as printed. Flagged for the user: reword A to 'Enable Person Accounts in Setup'. Separate note on citations — the deck's existing person-account self-registration link renders but is a stub that only points elsewhere, so the enablement article is the one carrying the facts.

question: Users logging into Salesforce are frequently prompted to verify their identity. The identity architect is required to provide recommendations so that the frequency of prompt verification can be reduced. What should the identity architect recommend to meet the requirement?
optionA: Implement 2FA authentication for the Salesforce org.
optionB: Implement multi-factor authentication for the Salesforce org.
optionC: Implement single sign-on for Salesforce using an external identity provider.
optionD: Set Trusted IP Ranges for the organization.
explanation:
Setting Trusted IP Ranges for the organization is the recommendation. Salesforce challenges a user to verify their identity when the login comes from a network it does not recognise; adding the corporate ranges under Network Access marks those logins as trusted, so the prompt stops appearing for anyone signing in from inside the network.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (implement 2FA for the org) — adds a required challenge to every login. It moves the frequency in the wrong direction.
Option B (implement multi-factor authentication for the org) — the same recommendation under the current name, and wrong for the same reason. Both A and B increase verification rather than reduce it.
Option C (implement single sign-on with an external identity provider) — moves authentication elsewhere but does not by itself tell Salesforce which networks to trust. Users can still meet identity verification, and the org gains a project rather than a fix.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_networkaccess.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has decided to replace the homegrown customer portal with Salesforce Experience Cloud. UC will continue to use its third-party single sign-on (SSO) solution that stores all of its customer and partner credentials. The first time a customer logs in to the Experience Cloud site through SSO, a user record needs to be created automatically. Which solution should an identity architect recommend in order to automatically provision users in Salesforce upon login?
optionA: Custom middleware and web services.
optionB: Custom login flow and Apex handler.
optionC: Just-in-Time (JIT) provisioning.
optionD: Third-party AppExchange solution.
explanation:
Just-in-Time provisioning is the recommendation. The third-party SSO solution already holds the credentials and can assert them, and JIT reads the attributes in that assertion to create the Experience Cloud user at the first login — which is exactly the moment the requirement names, with no code and no scheduled synchronisation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom middleware and web services) — builds an integration to do what the platform does natively on the login already taking place, and adds a component to host and monitor.
Option B (a custom login flow and Apex handler) — a login flow runs after Salesforce has authenticated the user, which for a first-time visitor means after the user record would already have had to exist. It is the wrong hook for creating one.
Option D (a third-party AppExchange solution) — introduces a purchased dependency for a capability included in the platform.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A group of users try to access one of Universal Containers' Connected Apps and receive the following error message: 'Failed: Not approved for access.' What is the most likely cause of this issue?
optionA: The Connected App setting 'All users may self-authorize' is enabled.
optionB: The Salesforce administrators have revoked the OAuth authorization.
optionC: The users do not have the correct profile or permission set assigned to them.
optionD: The use of High Assurance sessions is required for the Connected App.
explanation:
The users most likely do not have the correct profile or permission set assigned. 'Failed: Not approved for access' is the specific message a Connected App returns when its Permitted Users setting is 'Admin approved users are pre-authorized' and the person attempting access has not been granted the app through a profile or permission set. Assigning it resolves the error.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the setting 'All users may self-authorize' is enabled) — would produce the opposite behaviour. With self-authorization on, users are shown an approval screen and can grant access themselves, so this error would not appear.
Option B (administrators revoked the OAuth authorization) — a revoked authorization sends the user back through the approval process rather than refusing them outright, and it would not hit a whole group of users at once.
Option D (High Assurance sessions are required for the Connected App) — produces a different outcome: the user is prompted to raise their session by verifying their identity, not told they are not approved.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000386708&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000272761&language=en_US&type=1

question: A company with 15,000 employees is using Salesforce and would like to take the necessary steps to highlight or curb fraudulent activity. Which tool should be used to track login data, such as the average number of logins, who logged in more than the average number of times, and who logged in during non-business hours?
optionA: Login Report
optionB: Login History
optionC: Login Inspector
optionD: Login Forensics
explanation:
Login Forensics is the tool for this. It is the Salesforce Shield feature that aggregates login events into analytics rather than listing them — average number of logins, which users exceed that average, and logins outside business hours are the questions it is built to answer, which is what makes fraudulent activity visible across 15,000 employees.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Login Report) — a report over login data can list and group events, but it gives no baseline to compare against. Building averages and outlier detection by hand is the work Login Forensics already does.
Option B (Login History) — the underlying event log: who logged in, from where, when, and with what result. It is the raw material rather than the analysis, and reading anomalies out of it at this scale is impractical.
Option C (Login Inspector) — not a Salesforce feature under that name.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_monitor_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_login_history.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is using Experience Cloud as an Identity for its application on Heroku. The application on Heroku should be able to handle two brands, Northern Trail Shoes and Northern Trail Shirts. A user should select either of the two brands in Heroku before logging into the community. The app then performs authorization using OAuth 2.0 with the Salesforce Experience Cloud site. NTO wants to make sure it renders login page images dynamically based on the user's brand preference selected in Heroku before authorization. What should an identity architect do to fulfill the above requirements?
optionA: For each brand create different communities and redirect users to the appropriate community using a custom Login Controller written in Apex.
optionB: Create multiple login screens using Experience Builder and use Login Flows at runtime to route to different login screens.
optionC: Authorize the third-party service by sending authorization requests to the community-url/services/oauth2/authorize/cookie_value.
optionD: Authorize the third-party service by sending authorization requests to the community-url/services/oauth2/authorize/expid_value.
explanation:
Sending the authorization request to community-url/services/oauth2/authorize/expid_value is the answer. Salesforce lets the OAuth authorization endpoint be extended with an Experience ID, and that value is what drives dynamic branding — so the brand the user picked in Heroku travels with the authorization request and the login page renders that brand's images before authorization completes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a separate community per brand with a custom Apex Login Controller) — solves the problem by duplicating the site, doubling everything that must be built and maintained, and adds custom code to the login path for something the endpoint supports natively.
Option B (multiple login screens in Experience Builder routed by Login Flows) — a login flow runs after authentication, which is too late to brand the login page the user is looking at beforehand.
Option C (the same endpoint with cookie_value) — the right endpoint shape with the wrong parameter. Branding is resolved from the Experience ID; there is no cookie_value segment on the authorize endpoint.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_branding_use_cases.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.external_identity_dynamic_extend_endpoint_expid.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) believes a specific user account may have been compromised. NTO inactivated the user account and needs to perform a forensic analysis and identify signals that could indicate a breach has occurred. What should NTO's first step be in gathering signals that could indicate account compromise?
optionA: Download the Setup Audit Trail and review all recent activities performed by the user.
optionB: Review the User record and evaluate the login and transaction history.
optionC: Download the Login History and evaluate the details of logins performed by the user.
optionD: Download the Identity Provider Event Log and evaluate the details of activities performed by the user.
explanation:
Downloading the Login History and evaluating the details of the user's logins is the first step. It records source IP, login time, browser and platform, application, and whether each attempt succeeded — so unfamiliar geographies, odd hours or a new device show up immediately, and those signals scope everything the investigation looks at next.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the Setup Audit Trail) — records configuration changes made in Setup. It is worth reading if the account had administrative rights, but it says nothing about how or from where the account was accessed.
Option B (review the User record and its login and transaction history) — the User record itself carries no forensic detail, and 'transaction history' is not something the user record exposes. The login detail lives in Login History.
Option D (the Identity Provider Event Log) — records events for which this org acted as an identity provider, asserting identity to other applications. It would capture only a slice of the picture, and nothing at all unless the org is configured as an IdP.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_login_history.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_monitor_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has Active Directory (AD) as their enterprise identity store and would like to use it for Salesforce user authentication. UC expects to synchronize user data between Salesforce and AD and assign the appropriate Profile and Permission Sets based on AD group membership. What would be the optimal way to implement SSO?
optionA: Use Active Directory Federation Services (ADFS) as the Identity Provider.
optionB: Use Active Directory with Reverse Proxy as the Identity Provider.
optionC: Use Salesforce Identity Connect as the Identity Provider.
optionD: Use Microsoft Access Control Service as the Authentication Provider.
explanation:
Salesforce Identity Connect is the optimal implementation. It is the one option that delivers both requirements together: single sign-on from Active Directory, and synchronisation of user data with mapping from AD group membership to the right Salesforce profile and permission sets.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Active Directory Federation Services as the identity provider) — a genuine and common SSO answer, and it stops there. ADFS federates authentication but performs no user or group synchronisation into Salesforce, leaving half the requirement unmet.
Option B (Active Directory with a reverse proxy as the identity provider) — a reverse proxy relays traffic; it does not turn AD into a SAML identity provider, and it provides no provisioning either.
Option D (Microsoft Access Control Service as the authentication provider) — a retired Azure service, and an authentication provider handles inbound social or OpenID Connect logins rather than directory synchronisation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identityconnect_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An enterprise is using a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) server as the only point for user authentication with a username/password. Salesforce Delegated Authentication is configured to integrate Salesforce under single sign-on (SSO). How can end users change their password?
optionA: Users can click on the 'Forgot your Password' link on the Salesforce.com login page.
optionB: Users, once logged in, can go to the Change Password screen in Salesforce.
optionC: Users can request the Salesforce Admin to reset their password.
optionD: Users can change it on the enterprise LDAP authentication portal.
explanation:
Users change their password on the enterprise LDAP authentication portal. With Delegated Authentication, Salesforce never holds the password: every login attempt is forwarded to the LDAP service, which is the sole source of truth. The only place a change means anything is therefore the enterprise portal in front of that directory.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A ('Forgot your Password' on the Salesforce login page) — would reset a Salesforce password that is not being consulted. The next login still goes to LDAP with whatever the user types.
Option B (the Change Password screen in Salesforce once logged in) — the same problem from inside the session, and for delegated users this path is not the one that governs their access.
Option C (ask the Salesforce Admin to reset the password) — a Salesforce administrator has no reach into the LDAP directory, so there is nothing they can reset that would change how the user authenticates.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_delauthentication_tips.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is considering a Customer 360 initiative to gain a single source of truth for its customer data across disparate systems and services. UC wants to understand the primary benefits of Customer 360 Identity and how it contributes to a successful Customer 360 Truth project. What are two key benefits of Customer 360 Identity as it relates to Customer 360? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Customer 360 Identity enables an organization to build a single login for each of its customers, giving the organization an understanding of the user's login activity across all its digital properties and applications.
optionB: Customer 360 Identity automatically integrates with Customer 360 Data Manager and Customer 360 Audiences to seamlessly populate all user data.
optionC: Customer 360 Identity supports multiple brands so you can deliver centralized identity services and correlation of user activity, even if it spans multiple corporate brands and user experiences.
optionD: Customer 360 Identity not only provides a unified sign up and sign in experience, but also tracks anonymous user activity prior to signing up so organizations can understand user activity before and after the users identify themselves.
explanation:
Two benefits stand out. Customer 360 Identity gives an organisation a single login per customer, so one identity spans all its digital properties and applications and the login activity across them belongs to the same person. And it supports multiple brands, delivering centralised identity services while still letting each brand present its own experience — with user activity correlated across them rather than fragmented by brand.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (it automatically integrates with Customer 360 Data Manager and Customer 360 Audiences to populate all user data) — overstates the coupling. These are separate products with their own configuration; identity does not seamlessly fill them for you, and 'automatically' is doing work no documentation supports.
Option D (it tracks anonymous user activity before sign-up so activity is understood before and after identification) — describes anonymous-to-known tracking, which is marketing engagement territory rather than what the identity layer provides.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_licenses.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.external_identity_dynamic_multiple_brands.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has built a custom token-based Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) system for their existing on-premise applications. They are now implementing Salesforce and would like to enable a Two-Factor login process for it as well. What is the recommended solution an architect should consider?
optionA: Use the custom 2FA system for on-premise applications and native 2FA for Salesforce.
optionB: Use Custom Login Flows to connect to the existing custom 2FA system for use in Salesforce.
optionC: Replace the custom 2FA system with an AppExchange app that supports on-premise applications and Salesforce.
optionD: Replace the custom 2FA system with Salesforce 2FA for on-premise applications and Salesforce.
explanation:
Using Custom Login Flows to connect to the existing custom 2FA system is the recommended solution. A login flow runs between successful credential entry and the established session, and Apex inside it can call the on-premise verification service and refuse to complete the login until it answers. UC keeps the investment it has already made, and users meet one consistent second factor everywhere.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom 2FA on-premise and native 2FA in Salesforce) — gives users two different second factors to carry and two systems to enrol in, which is the split the question is trying to avoid.
Option C (replace the custom system with an AppExchange app covering both) — discards a working system and makes the on-premise applications depend on a purchased product, a far larger change than the requirement calls for.
Option D (replace the custom system with Salesforce 2FA for the on-premise applications too) — Salesforce's 2FA secures logins to Salesforce. It is not a verification service the on-premise applications can call, so this leaves them without a second factor at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_login_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers plans to develop a custom mobile app for the sales team that will use Salesforce for authentication and access management. The mobile app access needs to be restricted to only the sales team. What would be the recommended solution to grant mobile app access to sales users?
optionA: Use a custom attribute on the User object to control access to the mobile app.
optionB: Use the Permission Set License to assign the mobile app permission to sales users.
optionC: Add a new identity provider to authenticate and authorize mobile users.
optionD: Use Connected App OAuth policies to restrict mobile app access to authorized users.
explanation:
Connected App OAuth policies are the recommended way to restrict access. Setting Permitted Users on the connected app to 'Admin approved users are pre-authorized' means only people granted the app through a profile or permission set can authenticate through it — so assigning it to the sales team alone restricts the mobile app to exactly that group.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom attribute on the User object) — a field records an intention but enforces nothing. The OAuth flow does not consult it, so any user could still authorize the app.
Option B (a Permission Set License granting the mobile app permission) — a permission set license unlocks a feature set for a user; it is not the mechanism that authorizes a connected app, and there is no mobile app permission of this kind to assign.
Option C (add a new identity provider to authenticate and authorize mobile users) — adds a system to the login path without answering the question. Which users may reach the app is decided by the connected app's policies whichever provider authenticates them.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.connected_app_manage_oauth.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000272761&language=en_US&type=1

question: A company wants to provide its employees with a custom mobile app that accesses Salesforce. Users are required to download the internal native iOS mobile app from corporate intranet on their mobile device. The app allows flexibility to access other non-Salesforce internal applications once users authenticate with Salesforce. The apps self-authorize, and users are permitted to use the apps once they have logged into Salesforce. How should an identity architect meet the above requirements with the privately distributed mobile app?
optionA: Configure Mobile App settings in the Connected App and Salesforce as identity provider for non-Salesforce internal apps.
optionB: Create a new hybrid mobile app and use the Connected App with OAuth to authenticate users for Salesforce and non-Salesforce internal apps.
optionC: Use Salesforce as an identity provider (IdP) to access the mobile app and use the external IdP for other non-Salesforce internal apps.
optionD: Use Connected App with OAuth and Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) to access other non-Salesforce internal apps.
explanation:
Configuring the Mobile App settings in the Connected App, with Salesforce acting as identity provider for the non-Salesforce internal applications, meets these requirements. The Mobile App settings on the connected app are what support a privately distributed native iOS build authenticating to Salesforce; making Salesforce the IdP for the other internal applications is what lets those apps self-authorize once the user holds a Salesforce session, which is precisely the behaviour described.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (build a new hybrid mobile app and use a Connected App with OAuth) — replaces the native iOS app the requirement already specifies, and OAuth to Salesforce alone does nothing to sign the user in to the other internal applications.
Option C (Salesforce as IdP for the mobile app, an external IdP for the internal apps) — splits identity across two providers, so the user authenticates twice and the internal apps cannot self-authorize from the Salesforce session.
Option D (a Connected App with OAuth and SAML for the other internal apps) — names the right half of the mechanism for the internal applications and omits the mobile app configuration that makes a privately distributed native app work, which is the part the question is really asking about.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_saml_setting_up.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identity_provider_enable.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_saml_sso.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The security team at Universal Containers (UC) has identified exporting reports as a high-risk action and would like to require users to be logged into Salesforce with their Active Directory (AD) credentials when doing so. For all other uses of Salesforce, users should be allowed to use AD credentials or Salesforce credentials. What solution should be recommended to prevent exporting reports except when logged in using AD credentials, while maintaining the ability to view reports when logged in with Salesforce credentials?
optionA: Use SAML federated authentication with a login flow to dynamically add or remove a permission set that grants the Export Reports permission.
optionB: Use SAML federated authentication, treat SAML sessions as High Assurance, and raise the session level required for exporting reports.
optionC: Use SAML federated authentication and custom SAML JIT provisioning to dynamically add or remove a permission set that grants the Export Reports permission.
optionD: Use SAML federated authentication and block access to reports when accessed through a standard assurance session.
explanation:
Treating SAML sessions as High Assurance and raising the session level required for exporting reports is the solution. Salesforce lets each login method be assigned a session security level, so an Active Directory login arriving over SAML produces a High Assurance session while a Salesforce password login produces a Standard one. Raising the level required for Export Reports then permits the export in the first case and blocks it in the second, while leaving report viewing untouched for everyone.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a login flow dynamically adding and removing a permission set granting Export Reports) — reaches a similar result by churning permission assignments on every login, which is fragile, leaves the grant standing if a flow fails midway, and rebuilds what session levels already do declaratively.
Option C (custom SAML JIT provisioning adding and removing the permission set) — the same churn moved into the JIT handler, and worse placed: JIT runs on SAML logins, so it has no hook at all on the Salesforce-credential logins that need the permission removed.
Option D (block access to reports in a standard assurance session) — over-blocks. The requirement is that users on Salesforce credentials can still view reports and only exporting is restricted.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_overview_sessions.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.understand_mfa_high_assurance_login_session.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_session.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to integrate a web application with Salesforce. The UC team has implemented the OAuth Web Server authentication flow for the authentication process. Which two considerations should an architect point out to UC? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The web application should be hosted on a secure server.
optionB: The flow will not provide an OAuth refresh token back to the server.
optionC: The flow involves passing the user credentials back and forth.
optionD: The web server must be able to protect consumer privacy.
explanation:
Two considerations matter. The web application should be hosted on a secure server, because the Web Server flow authenticates the client with a consumer secret, and a secret is only a secret while it stays on a server the organisation controls — putting this flow in browser JavaScript or a distributed binary exposes it. And the web server must be able to protect consumer privacy: it ends up holding access and refresh tokens along with whatever user data it retrieves, so it becomes a target worth securing in its own right.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the flow will not provide a refresh token back to the server) — the opposite is true. Returning a refresh token to a confidential client is one of the main reasons to choose this flow.
Option C (the flow involves passing user credentials back and forth) — describes the username-password flow. Here the user types their credentials at Salesforce's own login page, and the application never sees them; it receives an authorization code instead.
